speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved:
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That a Select Committee composed of Messrs. Baker, BClarid, Boyer, Bradbury, Burrell, Hazen, Kyte, Lesperance, McKay, McCraney. Molloy, Murphy, Northrup, Sevigny, Warnoek and Wilson (Wentworth), be appointed to inquire into the prevention of the pollution of navigable waters and to consider all matters relating thereto, with power to send for persons, papers and records, to examine witnesses under oath, and to report from time to time.
He said: Hon. gentlemen will remember that a committee of this character was appointed at the last session of the House. That committee held a number of meetings and made a report to the House recommending that the Government be requested to call during the recess, a convention composed of the members of the committee, of representatives of the different provinces of Canada, of representatives of the International Waterways Commission and of representatives of the Conservation Commission, for the purpose of discussing this matter with a view of seeing what joint action might be taken between the provinces and the Dominion. That convention was called and met in the city of Ottawa on October 30 last. There were present the following representatives: the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell), the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury), Chairman of the Committee of the House on the subject, the hon. member for McLeod (Mr. Warnoek), and the hon. member for Brome (Mr. Baker); representing the province of Manitoba-Hon. Mr. Howden, At-

torney General; Prince Edward Island- Hon. Mr. Mathieson, Premier; British Columbia-Hon. William R. Ross, Minister of Lands; Quebec-Dr. E. P. Lachapelle, President of the Provincial Board of Health; Mr R S Lea, member of the Provincial Board of Health, and Dr. E. Elzear Pelletier, Secretary of the Provincial Board of Health; Saskatchewan-Mr. P. Aird Murray, Civil Engineer, and Dr. Maurice M. Seymour, Commissioner of Public Health; New Brunswick-Hon. Mr. Flemming, Premier; International Joint Commission Mr. C. A. Magrath and Mr. H. A. Powell,
K C. * Conservation Commission-Mr. James White and Dr. A. Hodgetts. Mr. Thomas P Owens was appointed secretary of the conference. There were no representatives present, I regret to say, from the provinces of Ontario, Alberta and Nova Scotia.
A good deal of discussion took place with regard to matters of public health in so far as navigable waters are concerned, and with regard to the jurisdiction of the respective provinces and of the federal authorities. It was brought prominently to the attention of the convention that the matter of the pollution of navigable streams constituting international boundaries was being considered by the Internationa Waterways Commission. It was very strongly pointed out that the question of the pollution of navigable waters is, brought down to its final analysis, a matter for international consideration and international agreement. In a great many cases the pollution of navigable waters in Canada is caused by towns 'and villages situated on waterways which form part of the international boundary line, such as the at. Lawrence river, the Detroit river, the waterways of the Great Lakes, the rivers St. John and St. Croix in the province of New Brunswick, land others. In order, therefore, that any regulations which might be passed with a view to preventing the pollution of these streams should be effective, it is necessary that similar legislation should be enacted by both countries, because if legislation were enacted by one country and not by another, while there might be some mitigation of the evil that undoubtedly exists, there would not be any effective means of totally doing away with
the source of trouble.
All these matters were discussed at the convention and the following resolutions adopted:
Moved by Mr. Howden, Manitoba, seconded by Mr. Flemming, New Brunswick:
This conference views with great satisfaction the study now being made, through the medium Of the International Joint Commission, appointed under the treaty between the United States and Canada of the 11th January, 1909, of the subject of the Pollution of International Waterways.
That the secretary be instructed to send a copy of the resolution to the International Joint Commission.
A resolution was also moved by Mr. Pelletier, of Quebec, seconded by Mr. Flemming, commending the valuable services rendered by Mr. Bradbury in relation to the prevention of the pollution of navigable waters and expressing appreciation of the efforts of the Special Committee of the House of Commons in reference to Bill No. 2 of the session of 1912-13. The conference suggested that a similar parliamentary committee should meet this session to continue the investigation. Another resolution, moved by Dr. Lachapelle, of Quebec, seconded by Mr. Seymour, of Saskatchewan, reads as follows:
Whereas in the past questions affecting sanitation and public health, to be dealt with concurrently by the federal and provincial authorities, amongst others the question ot protecting water courses from pollution, have suffered from the non-existence of a federal
department of health ;	.
This conference considers that the erection of a federal department of public health might well receive the early attention of the Dominion Government.
This conference believes that such a department would be of assistance in solving interprovincial problems as to the protection of public health.
Addresses were made by different gentlemen present, including specialists on the subject representing the provincial health authorities of the province of Quebec, one of the resolutions, as I have said, recommended the appointment of a committee at the present session to inquire into the pollution of navigable streams, and it" is in line with that recommendation that the appointment of this committee is now asked for. Until the report of the International Waterways Commission, which is investigating the pollution of international waters, is received, probably no progress can be made. But when we get that report, with the evidence of all the experts, it is hoped that with the co-operation of this committee and of this Parliament some practical solution may be worked out to remedy what is undoubtedly a very groat evil and a great menace to the public health of Canada to-day. Hon. GEORGE P. GRAHAM: Does not my hon. friend think there may be a disposition throughout the country to question the usefulness of the House of Commons if pass a Bill already passed bv -he Senate? I know the reverse of that has occurred. Sometimes the action of the Senate has been questioned because it wished to refer to the people themselves a measure passed by this House, and we must be careful not to get the House of Commons in a similar position.
This is a question of more than ordinary importance, and it has been before the public of Canada for a great many years. It will be .admitted that the International Waterways Commission has a very important connection with this subject so far as international streams are concerned, but the International Waterways Commission certainly has nothing to do with a stream like the Ottawa river, for instance. The provinces of Quebec and Ontario and the Dominion-of Canada are the only parties that can^ possibly be interested in the Ottawa river, and with all deference to the minister, it strikes me that this is merely sidestepping the issue. Our newspapers are full of the water question; we should have it at our meals if we dared drink the water; and it strikes me that the Government is not fulfilling its duty in postponing this matter any longer. If there is anything this Government, in conjunction with the Governments of the two provinces, can do, no time should be lost. The evil is here and has been here for years, with very disastrous results so far as this city	is concerned.
In dealing with streams wholly in Canadian territory the provinces must take a very important part through their board of health. I recollect that the water supply of various towns in Ontario has been absolutely condemned by the Provincial Board of Health; but it seerris that the matter

allow it to be put off for one year longer, for that is what it amounts to. I think our action would be universally approved if we at once took measures for dealing with this question of the pollution of streams in Canadian territory.
As to the question of pollution of international streams, that is, as my hon. friend says, a matter in which both countries are interested, and it is a very serious matter. Those of us who live on the St. Lawrence river think we have pure water, and, comparatively speaking, we have; but year by year as the population of the towns along its banks increases our water will become polluted. What are we going to do to remedy that? Are we going to sit still till the International Joint Commission does something? The Board of Health of the province of Ontario acts pretty strongly in these matters, and I think we should uphold their hands rather than shrink from our responsibility. There are many towns and incorporated villages in Ontario and other provinces that have no streams like the St. Lawrence running by them. They are under the control of the Board of Health and are taking care of the problem of sewage in a modern way. The longer this matter is delayed, the more expensive it will be to the people of this country, and I think the time has arrived for us to insist that no more sewage pipes be run into these streams. That is the first step. The next step would be for the people to take care of that question in another way just as soon as they could stand the taxation. I think, with all due respect to the hon. Minister of Marine and .Fisheries, we are not taking the proper course in side-stepping this great and important question for one more year; but we ought to take up the Bill which is now before the House and deal with it this year.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. L. BORDEN (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I think that my hon. friend (Mr. Graham) does not give proper credit to his own intelligence, if he understands my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and

Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) as suggesting that the International Joint Commission was to deal with problems which relate only to our own waters. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries was not alluding to the work of the International Joint Commission in that regard at all, but he was alluding to it in connection with the work which is properly within its scope, that is, the investigation of the condition of the international waterways between the two countries. It is only with that, in so far as I am aware, that the International Joint Commission has concerned itself up to the present time, or is likely to concern itself in the future.
The subject is of very great importance, and a committee was appointed at the last .session of Parliament to deal with it. My [DOT]hon. friend seems disposed to be rather captious about the matter. He says that it has already been delayed too long. I am not aware of any steps that were taken during the fifteen years of the Administration which preceded this.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: These gentlemen are so sensitive that if one refers to their record it disturbs them. They seem to be under the impression that the slightest reference to their record is an insult. I am not disposed to deny that, if my hon. friends look upon it in that way. I remember that the Bill now before the House, which has come from the Senate, was brought down under the late Administration, and that not the slightest notice was taken of it. My hon. friend was not so keen upon the responsibility of the Government then as he is now. He is capable of playing the petty part of trying to make a little political capital out of the matter if he can.
No, no.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
As far as I understood his observations, they could have no other purpose or object. The subject of this motion is one that should come properly under the consideration of a committee of this House, and I would be glad indeed if a committee of the Senate were added for the purpose of making a proper investigation, As my hon. friend has said', such conditions have been allowed to prevail in this country for so many years that it is yery difficult t-o reverse them by sudden legislation. That is no reason, however, why we should not proceed, after careful investigation and inquiry, to deal with
this subject in a reasonable and effective
I appreciate as much as my hon. friend does the very unfortunate condition that has prevailed in the city of Ottawa for several years, and I very greatly regret that during the past three or four years, while these conditions have prevailed, so little progress has been made by those who are responsible for the civic government in bringing about better conditions. In saying that I am making my observations entirely in a general sense, and they have application merely to the citizens as a whole, because I know there are a great many earnest persons, citizens of Ottawa, who have laboured most indefatigably and earnestly, and, I hope, effectively, to bring about a better condition in this city. The Government of Canada is very actively concerned in what has been done in Ottawa in that regard, because the large number of civil servants who reside in this city, the people who continually come here in connection with public business, and all the members of both Houses of Parliament who reside here during a portion of the year, are subjected to very great danger of infection unless we have a proper water supply. Indeed, it is conceivable that the whole public business of the country might be brought to a standstill by the enforcement of quarantine regulations; and I do express the hope now, in which I know that the members of this House will concur, that something will be done by the city of Ottawa in the immediate future to provide a suitable remedy for these conditions and to bring into the city an abundant supply of absolutely pure water.
As is disclosed by documents which have already been laid on the table of the House, the Government has pledged itself to submit to Parliament proposals for assisting in that purpose if it is absolutely assured that the supply of water will be both abundant and pure, because both of these are first considerations. As far as the appointment of a committee is concerned, it seems to be an absolutely correct motion at the present time. Indeed, the labours of the committee at the last session of Parliament, and the report which they made to the House, disclose, to my mind, the necessity of a full investigation and inquiry before we can deal effectively with this matter. I believe the thanks of the House and the country are due to those members of Parliament-Senator Belcourt in the Senate,' and my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) and others in this

House-who have undertaken at all times to impress the importance of this question *upon the attention of the House.

It was not my intention to intervene in this discussion; but I think it is due to the members of this House that I should clear up a misapprehension which seems to exist with reference to the cause of the typhoid epidemics that have occurred in Ottawa during the last few years. The discussion here this afternoon, as far as I could gauge it, has proceeded on the assumption that the epidemics were due to the pollution of the Ottawa river. As has been pointed out several times at investigations under oath these epidemics would have happened if the Ottawa river were as pure as distilled water could possibly be. These epidemics were not due to the water of the Ottawa river, but were caused by sewage being put into the water pipes supplying the city of Ottawa at the corner of Lloyd and Ottawa streets. The people were supplied with sewage instead of water, and I do not think that the condition of the water of the Ottawa river had anything to do with these epidemics.

I understood the remarks of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) exactly in the same sense as they were understood by my hon. friend from Renfrew (Mr. Graham), that is to say-if I am in error I want to be corrected-that while the Minister of Marine and Fisheries seemed to put great stress upon having a report as to the Ottawa river from the Waterways Commission, he believed that the first step to be taken was to preserve the purity of the St, Lawrence river, and that after this had been secured we could deal with our own water. I differ altogether with him in this respect. That was the reason why my hon. friend was justified in charging the Government with side-stepping this question. The hon. minister will not, after consideration, argue seriously that we must wait until action has been taken in regard to the St. Lawrence river, and that if no action is taken to get pure water in the St. Lawrence river, we shall not be able to take any action here. On the contrary, we can and we ought to take action immediately with regard to any of the waters over which we have jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I was not paying close
attention to what my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries said, but when 
the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) was speaking, I asked my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries whether he intended any such suggestion as that, and he told me that he certainlv did not.	*

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Well, I will
accept the correction.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: He (Mr. Hazen) is here now, and he can speak for himself.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Exactly. I was going to say in his presence what I said a moment ago. Am I right in understanding the Minister of Marine to have said that the first thing to be done was to regulate international streams? What about the Ottawa river?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I said that the question
in its widest aspect could not be dealt with except by international agreement, but 1 made no reference to the Ottawa river.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The first
stream to demand our attention is not the river St. Lawrence, because the volume of water in that river is so enormous that up to the present it has not become polluted, notwithstanding the sewage from municipalities which is poured into it; our first attention should be given to the waters over which we have jurisdiction, and one of these is the Ottawa river, from which we obtain our water supply here. The Bill of the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) could, I think, be voted upon right away, and the Bill of Senator Belcourt is almost similar in its terms. Is there a man in this House, including the Minister of Marine, who is of the opinion that in this age we should allow sewage to be put into any stream? The time has come for us to take action. We do not require any more investigation; we should have legislation at once to force all municipalities to dispose of their sewage in some other way. The only thing for us to consider now is whether or not we should give the municipalities time to get rid of their present systems; but I protest against any further deferring of prohibition against municipalities allowing their sewage to go into the rivers. I hold up both hands in support of the Bill of the hon. member for Selkirk. Why should we have a committee at this late date, to inquire whether we should allow pollution or not? I, of course, consent to the motion that Senator Beloourt's Bill and Mr. Bradbury's Bill should be referred to this committee, but I consent to it in the strong hope that the committee will report favour-

ably oil the passage of such a law. We have abundance.of water in the Ottawa river for the supply of the city. Let the Ottawa river be no longer polluted by sewage, and we shall have the best water in the world; there is none better. That is the whole question. I shall not allude to the usual refrain of hon. gentlemen opposite, that when we were in power we were not diligent in this matter, nor do I believe that that, if true, would be justification for the inaction of the present Government. I know that we had a hard battle to fight against the lumbermen of Ottawa, who insisted upon polluting the waters of the river with the refuse from their mills, and it took us years to get the mill-owners to correct their practice in that respect, but in the end we succeeded. If the late Government was not diligent, is that a reason why the present Government should be so dilatory. I am sick and tired, hearing these comparisons between the present Government and the late Government. So much was expected from this Government, so strong was the hope that the new broom would sweep clean, that the people of the country are disappointed at their constant excuse for dilatoriness, which every time is summed up by the retort: We are just as bad as you are. The elections will come by and by, and we will know what impression that excuse will make on the people of Canada.

I did not expect this question to come up to-day, but I feel that I should say a word or two about it. I have had a Bill on the Order Paper since the House opened, and I expected before this to have had opportunity to present it for a second reading. However, I heartily approve of the motion of the Minister of Marine to refer the Bill to a committee, although I regret that the motion was not made six or eight weeks ago.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Hear, hear;
see how dilatory they are over there.

This question is of
great importance to the people of the country; it is a question the solution of which affects the health and the lives of our people, and which ought to be dealt with in the most expeditious manner possible. There is no doubt that our streams are every day being polluted, and the committee appointed last year took a great deal of evidence from the best experts in Canada, who all agreed that some legislation ought to be passed by the federal Parliament to prevent this frightful nuisance. It was decided by that committee,
that a conference of the representatives of all the provinces should be convened, and last September that conference, attended by some of the premiers of the provinces, by the representatives of the boards of health, and by scientists and experts generally, met in Ottawa, and decided that the matter should be again brought before the House of Commons, and the committee of last year reappointed to take further evidence. I believe that decision of the conference was a wise one. But at this late period of the session, I do not know that we can hope to be very successful in getting evidence to warrant us in bringing down legislation this year. I had hoped that the matter would have come up earlier, and that we could have decided upon a Bill prohibiting this pernicious practice of polluting streams.
With regard to the water supply situation in the city of Ottawa, I think that the conditions in this city are a disgrace to civilization. To think that in a great city, the capital of the Dominion, the taxpayers should have to pay a heavy tax to the city for pure water, and then either have to buy their water for drinking purposes or carry it from wells to their homes, is an absurdity, inconsistent with modern ideas. I believe it has become quite evident that the officials of this city who are responsible for providing pure water for the inhabitants, are utterly incapable of doing so. This is the capital of the Dominion; we have a large number of representatives coming to Parliament for six or seven months in the year; we have thousands coming here to transact business with the Government and the departments; we have thousands of employees in the Civil Service, and I do not know that under the circumstances it would not be wise for the Government to undertake to provide pure water for this city. I believe the people of Canada would justify the Government if they took hold of this matter, and took it out of the hands of the city. I do not know just how it could be done.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Pass your Bill.

There is what appears to be a debatable question regarding obtaining the supply from the Ottawa river or from Thirty-One Mile lake. Personally I believe we have a body of absolutely pure water in Thirty-One Mile lake, which can be availed of for our supply, and knowing what has already taken place from the use of the Ottawa river water, I think we

should provide for taking our water from an unquestionably pure source. My hon. friend from Russell (Mr. Murphy) has stated that the Ottawa river water was polluted by the sewage from the city itself, and I believe he has ground for that charge. But I am not prepared to believe, that even with all the sewage from the city eliminated from the Ottawa river, that water is fit for the citizens to drink.
I do not believe that it is. In face of the evidence that we have, I believe that, if we adopt the Ottawa river water, a large quantity of chemicals will have to be used to purify the water. We are told that there is an opportunity of getting absolutely pure water for which no chemicals will be required. If the people of this country or of any country are to be healthy, they must have pure water to drink. I consider that the Government will be perfectly justified in taking hold of this matter and, if possible, in bringing pure water into this city in its own defence and in defence of the representatives who come here year after year. Only a short time ago it was suggested that this Parliament should adjourn until pure water was provided by the city of Ottawa. It is almost a duty devolving upon the Government of Canada to see that pure water is provided not only for their employees, hut for the members and others who are forced to. come to Ottawa to transact business. This is an important question, and one which I know has the sympathy of this House, and I am satisfied has the sympathy of the country. The Government that will legislate in a practical way to prevent the pollution of our streams will receive the commendation of the people of Canada.

This matter is very much more important in the western provinces than in any other part of the Dominion. In the western provinces, where water is less abundant than it is here, and where cities are now in the building, there exists first the necessity and then the opportunity to make provision for the future. No doubt it is desirable that there should be very full consideration of this question, not from the point of view that I understand the examination of last year was conducted. There is no question about the harmfulness of drinking polluted water.
The questions to be considered are the
scientific and economic possibilities, and I imagine that they must be considered in (conjunction with the provincial govern-

ments. The province cannot act alone, nor can the Dominion act alone. The question is a very great one, and without introducing controversial matters, I .would follow my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) by saying that, the matter having been brought up at last session, the Government is certainly entitled to censure for not having brought it forward for consideration at an earlier period of this session. But better late than *never; and I merely wish to emphasize what I said at first, that it is in the western provinces where the great opportunity and the great necessity for the work of preventing the pollution of streams lie to the hand of the Government, should they undertake that work.

I would like to say a word in regard to the two sides that this question assumes. There is the question of the pollution of waters, which may be and ought to be in the jurisdiction of the Dominion; but that the Dominion is to undertake the responsibility of providing pure water for the cities of Canada is another proposition, so wide that it frightens one when it presents itself.
The cities will pay for the water.

Is the Dominion to
mother all the cities of Canada and make them pay for the water?
Ottawa is the capital.
I know it is the capital, but we have municipal institutions in this country. Ottawa is under the municipal institutions of Ontario.
They do not seem to be able to provide pure water.

That may not be the fault of the municipal institutions, but of those living under them. If so, we ought to know it; but it is a most serious proposition to say that the federal authorities of a great country like Canada must undertake to make good the water of the various cities of the country. If that is the proposition, I want to have it fully discussed. But I agree with the hon. gentleman in saying that the [DOT] pollution of waters is a federal question, and the cities which pollute the water ought to be prevented from so doing. In the city of Toronto, we are doing it now in a way: we are putting the sewage into the bay and we are pumping the water from the -bay. Now we have a system by which we hope to get the water

for the city away down the lake where it cannot he contaminated. If this city is doing wrong in that respect, it ought to he stopped. If the towns up the Ottawa river pollute the water of that river, they ought to be prevented from doing so. It does not seem to be good doctrine to allow everybody to pollute the water, and then have a generous paternal Government provide pure water for every city that requires it. I would like to have enunciated a clear-cut policy in the matter

It is very refreshing to see the House of Commons diverted from the consideration of commercial questions to the discussion of the question before us to-day-one to my mind of very much greater importance than most of the questions on which we are spending our time in this House, the question of the lives and the physical well-being of the citizens of this country. It is gratifying to me, as I know it will be to a very large percentage of the citizens of this country, to see that the Parliament of Canada is waking up to the fact they have a great duty to perform to our citizens in respect of the preservation and the conservation of their health and physical welfare.
I am very glad that the Government are taking just the course that they propose of referring these Bills to a special committee of the House. We had a committee last year dealing with this matter, and a good foundation was laid for the continuation of the investigation this year. We got a good deal of information, which will be very valuable, and we are prepared to receive further information this year which will be still more valuable. For example, the medical officer of the Conservation Commission of Canada, as well as the provincial medical health officer of Ontario, visited Great Britain during the past summer. I believe that, when the committee meets, it will receive from these officers a report on the conditions as they found them in the old land, and especially on the question of the disposal of sewage when not put into streams and waters. This information seems to me very important, and I think that when the right hon. the leader of the Opposition and the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr Graham) ask this House immediately to vote on these Bills and pass them, they are doing so without knowing what that means. These Bills refer not only to the Ottawa and St. Lawrence rivers, but to every stream in the Dominion of Canada. This
is a matter affecting not only the city of Ottawa, but every town and village situ, ated on the inland streams of our country, because, when these Bills are passed, no sewage can be put into a stream which flows into a navigable stream. When these gentlemen ask that these Bills be passed at once, they are asking that something be done which is going to create very great difficulties for our municipalities, for this reason, that, so far as we know, tljere is no system for the disposal of sewage at present known which we are confident will be entirely satisfactory to the towns and cities of this northern country. With our severe winter and heavy frost, it is recognized by all sanitary engineers that it will be very difficult to find a satisfactory method. We all agree that our streams and drinking water should not be polluted; but when we stop the placing of sewage in our streams, what is to be done with it? There immediately arises this very serious question; and before we ask our villages and towns, especially our smaller centres, to expend from $15,000 to $100,000 each for a sewage disposal plant, this Parliament, I think, ought to be in a position to recommend to these municipalities a system which, when erected, will be absolutely satisfactory. We cannot afford to have our municipalities experimenting in this matter for fear that, after experimenting, they will find that all their expenditure has been useless. That is a serious matter, and one upon which this committee can do a great deal to enlighten our people, and which, before these Bills are passed, should be dealt with by this Parliament.
If the epidemic of typhoid in Ottawa two years ago has aroused this Parliament to its duty in this matter, then perhaps that epidemic may not have been without benefit. But, while it was a serious visitation, let us not forget that every year in Canada from 2,000 to 2,500 people die from typhoid fever. Many of these cases are caused by impure water. Practically every one of these lives could be saved if the Parliament of Canada did its duty, and if the people of Canada were awake to the fact that these lives could be saved and that typhoid is a disease which can be eradicated if proper measures are taken to preserve
4 p.m. the health of the people. This matter is sufficiently important to claim the time and attention of this Parliament, even if no other feature in connection with the health of the people were to be considered.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. D. HAZEN (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
My right hon. friend who leads the Opposition (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has urged this measure as though it were a question that could be dealt with very easily and expeditiously. In fact, the right hon. gentleman has given the impression-I think he said it in so many words-that he sees no reason why the Bill of the hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bradbury) should not be voted on without further consideration, except such as might be given in Committee of the Whole House. It is somewhat surprising to note the contrast between the easy and airy way in which the right hon. gentleman disposes of great questions with a wave of his hand now that the re-ponsibilty of government has been removed from his shoulders, and the deliberation and consideration which he insisted upon for im portant measures of this kind, when he was Prime Minister, and chiefly responsible for the legislation of this House. It seems to me that in submitting seriously to this House the contention that this measure should be voted upon practically at the present time the right hon. gentleman shows that he has not given the subject due consideration. If this measure were adopted, the result would be that no raw sewage could be discharged into any navigable water in any part of Canada. Let us consider that for a moment. Is the House prepared to say that there are no navigable waters in Canada into which sewage should be discharged? Is the House to say that the raw sewage shall not be discharged into salt water in places where there is a large rise and fall of the tide, where these waters are not used for domestic purposes, and where no harm whatever is done by the discharge of sewage of towns and cities? Yet, under the Bill which the right hon. gentleman says he will vote for at once, no sewage could be discharged in a raw state into any navigable water in Canada; and so the towns and cities on the seacoast which, at great expense and under legislative authority, have provided means to discharge their sewage into these waters would be prevented from doing so two years after this Bill were passed. I would call attention to the fact that while raw sewage is being discharged into many of the waters of Canada which have to be used for domestic purposes, yet there are towns in Canada which, in discharging their sewage into these waters, subject it to a certain amount of treatment before it is discharged. That is true, I might say to the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), of a good many 
towns in the West. And before a Bill is passed which will prevent these towns from discharging their sewage into these navigable waters, surely means ought to be taken to find out whether the method of sewage treatment adopted by them is sufficient to purify the sewage to such an extent that its discharge into the waters is harmless; that is, that its effect is not poisonous and does not interfere with the use of these waters for domestic purposes.

Would the hon. minister
please say which cities treat their sewage as he has indicated?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
When a Bill similar to this was before the House last year, I gave a general statement of how the different towns throughout Canada were discharging their sewage and what they were doing with it. From that statement, I take the following
Brandon discharges its sewage into the Assiniboine, Carman into the Boyne river, Portage la Prairie into the Assiniboine, St! Boniface into the Red river. In the case of Souris, the river is not named, Winnipeg discharges into the Red river and Assiniboine river. In no case is the sewage treated, but I And in regard to Souris that it is proposed to put in a filtration system. The provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta seem to be rather ahead of the other provinces in this matter in that they are making provision, and in some cases have made provision for treating the sewage before it is discharged into the water. At Moosejaw, the sewage which runs into the Moosejaw creek is treated in septic tanks. Prince Albert discharges its sewage into the North Saskatchewan river, and I have no record of any treatment of it. At Regina, there is treatment by means of septic tanks, sedimentation, disinfection tanks and biological filters. Saskatoon discharges its sewage into the South Saskatchewan river and has sewage disposal works under construction at the present time. In Alberta, Calgary discharges its sewage into the Bow river, Edmonton into the North Saskatchewan river, and part of the sewage of that city is treated in septic tanks. Lethbridge discharges into the Belly river and there a sewage purification plant is to be installed at once. The sewage of McLeod goes in to the Old Man river, and nothing is said about treating the sewage there. Medicine Hat discharges into the South Saskatchewan river, and has a sewage plant under consideration. Red Deer discharges into the Red Deer river and has a purification plant under consideration. Wetaskiwin discharges into Bigstone creek and is proposing to erect sewage disposal works.
This information, I may say, I obtained principally from the Commission of Conservation. It would be a great injustice to the people of various towns, who have expended money in the erection of plants for the purifying of sewage, if we were simply to pass a bald law stating that no sewage shall be deposited in any of the

navigable rivers throughout the country. All this will require the very greatest possible consideration. The interests of towns discharging sewage into navigable waters which are salt or unfit for domestic use, and the interests of those towns which have gone to the expense of installing sewage treatment plants, will all have to be considered, and scientific opinion would have to be obtained as to the efficiency of the sewage treatment in these particular towns before this legislation would be justified in interfering with the rights that these towns have exercised by legislative enactment for the purpose of discharging their sewage under the conditions mentioned. It would not be a troublesome thing, now or at any time, to pass a law providing that in future no raw sewage should be discharged into any navigable waters used for domestic purposes. But by doing that you would not be striking at the root of the evil, because many of the streams throughout the country are so filled with sewage that has been discharged into them that the prevention of further sewage being put in would do little to minimize the evil which exists to-day. There are, therefore, more things to be considered than simply the question of preventing the placing of more sewage into the streams. What would be the result if, at one stroke, we were to say to various cities and towns throughout Canada, as has been pointed out by the hon. gentleman who last addressed the House, that they must tear up the sewage plants which they have installed under legal authority, and find some other way of disposing of their sewage? Take the case of Montreal, with a population of about 600,000 inhabitants. If this Bill should become law, within two years that city would have to dispose of its sewage in some other way than by discharging it into the river St. Lawrence. I quoted figures last year to the House and to the committee-figures, the authenticity of which, I think, can be relied upon-to the effect that in a city like Montreal it would cost at least 86 per head of population to change their sewage system to some other system under which the sewage would be treated in septic tanks, by sedimentation or some other process. Would it be fair and right to ask Montreal to spend $3,600,000, which is the amount it would have to spend in order to make the change, without considering whether or not more time ought to be given within which to change the system which they have adopted in a perfectly legal manner, under the laws 111
cf the provincial legislature, and to consider what system they ought to adopt for the purpose of dealing with their sewage? The same applies to Toronto, and to very many cities	in	Ontario and Quebec. My right hon. * friend's suggestion that this matter should be disposed of without any further consideration shows, as I have said, that he has himself given very little consideration to the subject. That was not the view taken by the convention that met in Ottawa last year, a convention composed of scientific and public men representing most of the different provinces of Canada, who, after full discussion, passed a resolution to the effect that the matter should be further considered by a Committee of the House of Commons. In view of the immense sums of money that have been invested by different towns and municipalities, under the authoTty of law, for the disposal of sewage by having it flow into navigable streams, and in view of the other questions involved, I submit that it is only right and proper that the most careful consideration should be given to the matter, and that we should not hastily pass a Bill like that of the hon. member for Selkirk, which, passed in its present form, would undoubtedly do a great injury and wrong to the different cities throughout this country, and might not accomplish the very desirable object which the hon. gentleman has so much at heart. For these reasons, I submit that the right course has been taken in asking that this committee be again appointed.
What steps have the Government since taken in line with the resolution of last session?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Government took the
step that was recommended by this House. In the month of October it called together the convention which this House recommended should be called. If my hon. friend had been in the House when I moved the resolution, he would have heard me read the report of what occurred at that convention, the names of the delegates who were present, and the different resolutions which they adopted. Amongst the resolutions they adopted was one urging that at this session of the House the committee should be again appointed for the purpose of giving further consideration to the matter.
I would like to suggest an amendment.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
There cannot be any
amendment now.

It would be adopted
unanimously, I am quite sure.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The submitting of an
amendment now would be a violation of the rule, which provides that the mover of a substantive motion closes the debate wnen he makes his reply. The announcement was made to the House that if any hon. gentleman desired to speak he would have an opportunity of doing so before the mover closed the debate.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I understood that the minister himself was going to move that the Bill of the hon. member for Selkirk be referred to the committee.
Mr. HAZEL': It was my intention to move, when the Bill from the Senate comes before the House, that it should be referred to this committee, and that the Bill of the hon. member for Selkirk also should be referred to the committee. It makes no difference when it is done; I would just as soon do it now as at any other time; but I did not intend to make such a motion a part of the resolution which is now before the House.
Perhaps the House may consent to my offering the amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: If my hon. friend's amendment is that these Bills should be referred to this committee, I am quite willing to accept it.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Bills are not now before the House; therefore it would be quite irregular to move such an amendment. In my judgment, it would be quite in order to do so when the Bills are before the House.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I do not know when the Bills will be before the House. The Bill of the hon. member for Selkirk will not, under the rules of the House, be called this session.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: We may have the Bills called by consent of the House.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
We can do
anything by consent.
Motion of Mr. Hazen agreed to.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Although the Bill has not been called, what objection could there be to a motion that the Bill of the hon. member for Selkirk, which is on the Order Paper, be referred to this committee?
fMr. Lemieux.]

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: If it were desired to refer these Bills to the committee, I think the proper way would be to move to have the Bills called, and then make the necessary motion. That could be done now, or at some future time.

I see that there is an abundance of consent, Mr. Speaker. I beg
to move:
That Bill No. 5, and Bill No. 106, letter B of the Senate, respecting the Pollution of Navigable Waters, be referred to the said committee.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: I move that these Bills be now called, for the purpose of hawing them referred to the committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Before the Bill can bereferred to this committee, it must be read a first and a second time. That has not been done.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
We might do that
with the consent of the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If an hon. member will make a motion that Bill No. 5, Public Bills and Orders, be now called, we can go on in the regular way.
Mr. PELLETIER thereupon moved that Bill No. 5, Public Bills and Orders, be now taken up.

speakerposition: stagedirection

Motion agreed to.
Mr. BRADBURY moved the second reading of Bill No. 5, respecting the Pollution of Navigable Waters. He said: In moving the second reading of this Bill I desire to say a word or two.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think that could only be done with the consent of the House, because this Bill is being taken up out of its order for one purpose only viz. to refer it to this committee. I understood the object was merely to refer the Bill to the committee.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and referred to the committee appointed to consider the question of the pollution of navigable waters.
Mr. PELLETIER, with the consent of the House, moved that Bill No. 106, letter B of the Senate, be next considered.
Motion agreed to.
Mr. PELLETIER thereupon moved the first reading of Bill No. 106, respecting the Pollution of Navigable Waters.

Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

speechtext:
The second reading can only be taken with the unanimous consent of the House.

speakerposition: stagedirection

On motion of Hon. W. T. White (Minister of Finance) the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Blondin in the chair:
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Civil Service Insurance Act, chapter 18, of the Revised Statutes, 1906, and to provide that the minister may contract with any person to whom Part 1 of the Civil Service Superannuation and Retirement Act applies on the first day of April, one thousand nine hundred and fourteen, or who was appointed to a permanent position in any branch of the public service of Canada, whether civil or military, after the first day of April, one thousand eight hundred and ninety-three, for the payment of a certain sum of money to -be made upon the death of such person ; that further provision be made as to the apportionment of insurance among beneficiaries ; that the minimum and maximum amounts payable at death shall be one thousand dollars and five thousand dollars respectively, and that moneys received shall form part of, and moneys payable shall he paid out of the Consolidated Revenue Fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There are two chief features in the Bill which I shall introduce following the adoption of the resolution. One is 1114
that female members of the Civil Service are made eligible for insurance under the Act, so that the sexes are placed upon an equality in .that regard. The other is that the maximum amount of insurance payable upon death is increased from $2,000 to $5,000.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Are these the only features of the legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There is a further provision for the apportionment of the insurance in the event of the death of the insured. There are no other important features of the resolution.
Some people have insured up to the maximum of $2,000 and have retired from the service. Can they, under this proposed legislation, increase their insurance up to the maximum of $5,000?	,

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The wording of the said Act is as follows:
Section 13 of the said Act is repealed,-
That section refers to the minimum and maximum amounts payable at death, which, under the existing legislation, are $1,000 and $2,000 respectively.
-and the following is substituted therefor: The minimum and maximum amounts payable at death which may be provided lot-under this Act shall be $1,000 and $5,000 respectively.
This new section takes the place of the old one. Offhand, I am not prepared to say whether the insured persons mentioned by my bon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) would be permitted to increase the amount of their insurance or not. That is a matter that has to do with the interpretation of this amendment. I shall look into it, and if it is considered proper that they should be so permitted, we can make the necessary amendment to the Bill.

On motion of Hon. Martin Burrell. (Minister of Agriculture), the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Blondin in the Chair:
Resolved, that it is expedient to consolidate and amend the laws relating to dairy pro-

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: ducts, and to prohibit the manufacture or sale of butter substitutes.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The Bill to be founded upon this resolution is to make a revision of Part 8 of the Inspection and Sale Act, which was a consolidation of all the dairy laws previous to that time. We take it out of the Inspection and Sale Act as a matter of convenience, because it practically has nothing to do with the general terms of that Act and especially with Part 1, which applies to the whole of the operations with respect to the Inspection and Sale Act. It is much more convenient in administration to have a separate Dairy and Sale Act. There are some amendments of this Act, bringing it up to the different terms of the dairy industry which have been modernized and expanded in the last few years. There are also some rather important clauses dealing with the manufacture of butter substitutes, because the old law was so weak that we never could secure convictions against a large number of people, notably in Montreal, who were putting an excessive amount of water in butter, the amount going as high as 40 and 50 per cent. The judge held that under the old section of the Act we had not the proper authority to convict; so that we are remedying that. The other provisions I can explain when the Bill is printed and the second reading comes up.
There are no more radical changes?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
No more radical changes.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. BURRELL thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 112, to regulate the manufacture and sale of dairy products and to prohibit the manufacture and sale of butter substitutes.

speakerposition: stagedirection

On motion of Hon. Martin Burrell (Minister of Agriculture), the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Blondin in the Chair:
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide for the control and inspection of cold storage warehouses and food products preserved in cold storage.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The Bill with which
this resolution is concerned, is drawn for the purpose of exercising reasonable con-IMr. Burrell.]
trol and supervision over cold storage warehouses. The Bill will provide for the making of regulations, dealing with such things as licensing cold storage warehouses, the inspection of the food products therein, or after they have been removed from the warehouse, the compelling of returns of the quantities in storage by the owners, and for purposes such as limiting the time of 'Storage. Last year, Senator Taylor had a Bill dealing with cold storage matters before the Senate, and it was withdrawn on the understanding that the Government would take the matter up. This session, my hon. friend from Selkirk also has a Bill on the Order Paper dealing with the matter, and I understand that my hon. friend is willing to withdraw his Bill, in view of the proposal of the Government. I need nardly say to him that the Government will gladly adopt in this Bill such provisions as may be applicable to the legislation, and listen to any suggestions which he, in common with any other members of the House, may make.
Is it a long Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: No.

I consider this to be
one of the most important Bills of the session. For months and months the people of Canada, in view of the hign cost of living, have been blaming the cold storage warehousemen foT exacting high prices for products, and I should like to know if there will be any provision in the Bill forcing the cold storage people to sell their products at fixed periods. When my hon. friend from Selkirk introduced his Bill at the beginning of the session, I promised nim my earnest support, but unless the Bill now proposed by the minister is as stringent as that introduced by the -hon. member, I would not promise him the same isupporfc.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
The main provisions of this Bill are to give power to .make regulations dealing with the subjects the hon. gentleman has mentioned. I do not want to discuss now the reasons why it was deemed more advisable to do by a regulation than by specific mention within the four cornel's of the statute, but there are no good reasons. The Bill will give us power to make regulations concerning the very things, my hon. friend '(Mr. Lemieux) has referred to, but I think it would be very much better to leave further discussion until the Bill is printed when I will give a com-

plete statement, and ask that the Bill be referred to such committee as may give its provisions through ventilation. Our object is not to make it unnecessarily drastic, so as to cripple any justly established industry, but at the same time to give proper control over a thing connected so intimately with the food supply of the people.
Are there in force in the United States any such regulations as the minister will propose?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Individual states have passed legislation, some of which work well and some of which do not. It is largely in the experimental stage.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Mr. BURRELL thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 113, to regulate cold storage warehouses.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.'

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: On motion of Hon. W. B. Nantel (Minister of Inland Revenue), Bill No. 96, to amend the Weights and Measures Act, was read the second time, and the House went into committee thereon, Mr. Blondin in the Chair. .
Will the minister give a general statement as to the purpose of this Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I explained on the first reading that the only object of the Bill is to substitute the meter and kilogram of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures for the standards now used in the Department of Inland Revenue.
Does this mean that the metric system is making any progress in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Certainly. This law is urgently requested by the universities and the scientists of the Dominion. The metric system has been found very applicable to the measurements of electricity, and at present we are obliged to send to Paris to have comparison made with the original standards deposited there. When the Bill passes we will have these standards deposited in Ottawa, and the comparison can be made in the Department of Inland Revenue.

Does the Government intend to adopt the metric system in full? some years ago, when Mr. Justice Brodeur was Minister of Inland Revenue, he distributed throughout the country samples of weights and measures according to the metric system.
I understand that he began his campaign of education by distributing them to the various educational institutions of the country, so that the people would come to understand the system which is acknowledged in Europe to-day to be the best and most perfect system. We all know that a change in weights and measures is always attended with many difficulties. In fact, if any one travels to-day in France, he will find in some of the old communes and villages people who still use not only the expressions but the measures themselves of the old regime. There have been three changes in France in three centuries, and yet there are people there who still use the old measurements which were in use at the time of the monarchy in France.
In Canada, in the province of Quebec, as my hon. friends, especially those who belong to the legal profession know, there are people in our villages who still use the old expressions, so many ' francs,' so many ' louis,' and others who use the old English system, that we had about fifty years ago, when we adopted the American system of currency. I mention these things only to emphasize the fact that any change in weights and measurements is a very difficult problem indeed.
What progress has been made, and what are the intentions of the Government with regard to the metric system? Will that system some day, not too far distant, be made compulsory, or will the campaign of education begun some years ago, be proceeded with? The object of my hon. friend's Bill is to adopt one feature of the metric system. I understand that the provisions of this Bill apply to the classes mentioned a moment ago by my hon. friend, especially electrical instruments, and instruments used by engineers. Certain new instruments in engineering have recently been invented, and the metric system is universally used in connection with them. But this is only one phase of the question. Will my hon. friend inform the House whether or not the,metric system proper is to be made compulsory at no distant date?

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
This Bill is in that
direction. The metric system is used universally in electricity. It is not the in

tention of the Government to have the metric system made compulsory, in trade generally. When the people are properly educated to the fact that the metric system is more accurate than the old system, we will consider the advisability of making it compulsory. It is the intention of the department- to have a distribution made of the metric system, in order to make it known to the people as the best system. We do not at present consider it advisable to make the metric system compulsory in business generally.

I have listened with a great deal of interest to the observations of the minister in respect to the metric system. I cannot profess to understand the necessity for this change in the law, but I presume that there is a good reason for it. The statement of the hon. minister, if I understand him aright, that there was a proposition to make the metric system compulsory in Canada, is more serious. The question of measures, of how people shall calculate the weight or quantity of anything they have to sell, such as lumber, boards, or anything else that is to be measured 'Superficially by feet or yards, is a very important one in this country. It is a question that enters largely into the education of the people; it is a question strictly of education. Therefore it is a question not belonging altogether to this Parliament, but a provincial one. Consequently the minister should move very cautiously in creating any revolution in this country by adopting the metric system for the Dominion while it is not the system recognized by the different provinces.
The old style of currency of pounds, shillings -and pence, is not yet dead in the province from which I come. In the province of Newfoundland I am told that the people do a great deal of business in pounds, shillings and pence. I am told that they buy their cattle in dollars and cents, because it sounds better to say, 'I will give you $12 for your cow,' but that when selling they -say, 'I only ask three pounds.' Thus it 'sounds better to buy in dollars and to sell in pounds. I wish to .bring to the notice of the minister that ithose old institutions are very firmly fixed, ami, if he would ask men in the lumber yards of the province of Nova Scotia to sell their lumber by the metric system, there would be war. They would take years to get used to it.
I have no doubt at all about the beauty and scientific nicety of the method. 1

believe that it is a first-rate' system, highly scientific and highly educative. At the same time, I would urge upon the minister that he should not move too fast in compelling the old Scotchmen in the province of Nova Scotia to educate themselves in the use of that system.

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
It is in no way the intention of the department to have the metric system made compulsory. But the department considers that it is committed to the acceptance of the system to the degree now proposed. In 1907, Canada became a member of the International Conference of Weights .and Measures, an association now composed of twenty-seven nations, whose object is to study and control weights and measures according to the metric system; and Parliament every year voted $400 as a contribution to that conference and to the International Bureau. That International Bureau, by study, has discovered that there is a discrepancy between the meter which we have in the department and the one deposited in the Ihternational Bureau in France. So, we wish to have exact copies of the meter and kilogram now deposited with the bureau in France. That is the reason for the present Bill.	' -
' i

Of the twenty-seven
nations, excluding Canada, are all governed by the metric system of weights and measures?

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Some of them have declared it compulsory, and, with the exception of Canada and one or two others, all the others have adopted some such legislation as the measure now before the House.

Do all these nations
adopt this system merely for the purpose of the International Conference, or generally?

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
They have adopted it
because they consider it the best system. There is a treaty amongst these nations, one of the obligations of which is to adopt the metric system standards of the International Bureau.

There is no question about the great convenience of the use of the metric system as compared with the system we now have. At the same time, there seems no possibility of securing the adoption of the metric system by simply making a statutory declaration that it may be adopted or ought to be adopted. It

seems to me that what my hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) suggested is the only way. Until the provinces take the matter up and provide that the children in the schools shall be taught the metric system as a part of their education we cannot make very much progress. We certainly cannot force the system upon the people when they are not ready for it. The alternative is to get them ready for it by educating them in the schools. This action, of course, can only be taken by the provinces. My suggestion would be that the matter be discussed by this Government with the governments of the
5 p.m. provinces with a view to having the study of the metric i?ys-tem made a part of the arithmetical course in the schools. It would be no serious matter, a very trifling matter; and if the children were made acquainted with the system, then when they grew up, realizing its great convenience, they would of course be ready and willing to adopt it.

Has the British Government considered the advisability of adopting the metric system ? I remember that some years ago a Bill was introduced in the House of Commons in England, in which a date was fixed for the compulsory use of this system. There was a long discussion on the Bill; but I do not recall what became of that measure. My hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), I think, has gone to the very root of the matter. If the education of the people in the metric system goes on only as it has gone on for some years past, not much progress will be made. The progress of education has been, so to speak, spasmodic. When I was a private member on the other side of the House, durng the first years I was in Parliament, I made a request of the then Minister of Inland Revenue to secure instruments in use for the metric system that 1 might furnish them to the various academies and colleges with which I wias more or less connected. I did secure this distribution to a number of colleges and academies, but this method is not very satisfactory. As my hon. friend from Edmonton says, if the Government intends to have this system made the law of the land, a decided effort should be made with the provincial authorities to have the system made part of the educational curriculum in the various provinces. The metric system is to-day almost universally used. A few
countries have so far resisted, including Great Britain, but even in these countries the question is very seriously considered. But if in Canada we intend to adopt the system, a decided movement must be begun. The duty of the Government, it seems , to me, is to make arrangements with the provincial authorities so as to make as wide an advertisement of the metric system as possible through the public schools. This is a matter, perhaps, more provincial than federal. Of course, the weights and measures system is, by the constitution, placed under federal control. But education appertains to the various provinces, and through the provincial authorities the effort should be made to make the system as widely known -as possible. As my hon. friend from North Cape Breton stated, there is no prejudice so deeply rooted in the minds of the people, not only in the rural sections but in the cities, as that against any change in the system of weights and measures. As I stated ia moment ago, there are people in France to-day who still use the measurements which were in use under the monarchy; there are people in the provinces of France who speak of ' tant l'aulne,' while in other parts the metric system is in common use. In the province of Quebec land is still sold by the habitants	for so many	francs,	or
so many louis, or so many sterling. The old measures, weights and currencies are deeply rooted in the minds of the people, and if we want to have a new system we will have to teach the very youngest people from the start. Otherwise, the effort will be spasmodic and' of no consequence, and the Government will be spending money on this metric system with no result.	Unless there is a
well-defined policy; unless the young people are provided with the means of studying the system and of incorporating it, so to speak, into their education, I do not think the metric system will ever be used in Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: England and Denmark are the only nations of Europe that have not adopted a metric system, but in 1897 the use of the system was declared permissible in England.

What about the United
States ?

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It is permissible in the United States. It is used in matters connected with science, electricity, and international commercial relations.
Where is the central office of this bureau ?

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
At Sevres, a suburb of Paris.
Mr. MARCILE. A few years ago we had in our province a metric system of weights and measures. I received a letter yesterday from officers of the academy at St. Liboire, asking whether it is possible for the department to furnish the academy with maps and scales such as were used a few years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I will attend to that request.
Bill reported, read the third time, and passed.

On the first reading the right hon. leader of the Opposition and,
I think, some other members suggested that the provisions of the Act should come into force at an earlier date, and I promised to consider the matter. Some manufacturers whom I have seen since have urged that the time should be lengthened; others have urged that at any rate it should not be lessened.
