If we could get pure
water in Ottawa and get rid of white phosphorus in Hull, this would be a good place to live in. I think the Minister of Labour is getting on faster with white phosphorus than he is with pure water.

I would suggest to the minister that if the use of white phosphorus is prohibited at the end of two years, another year should be allowed for the distribution of the matches then manufactured.
On section 4-importation prohibited:
What does this mean?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Matches made of white phosphorus will be excluded.
On section 6-petition for compulsory license:

This seems to deal largely with applications for patents. Has the

minister considered possible collision between these sections and the Patents Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
The most general substitute for white phosphorus in countries where that is prohibited is a substance known as sesqui-sulphide of phosphorus, a compound of sulphur and phosphorus. That substance was patented in this country and later was assigned to the Diamond Match Company in the United States. The patent has since lapsed, owing to nonpayment of the fees, so that any one is free to use sesqui-sulphide now. There are ten or twelve other substances used as substitutes. Some of these are patented, and this provision is put in so that other people may secure a license to use these substances already patented. A similar provision is in the English Act. I do not think there will be any collision with the Patents Act.
On section 7-regulations:

Under this section the Governor in Council can almost make a new law. The efficiency of this Act will depend largely on the recommendations made by the Governor in Council. Subsection 3 provides that every such order or regulation ' shall be published in the Canada Gazette. With all due deference to the Canada Gazette, that is not real notice to the people who are interested. Of course, if they were looking out for the regulations, or had a lawyer watching for them, they might find them in the Canada Gazette, but as a matter of giving information to the people interested, the regulations might be buried in the Canada Gazette. I suppose, in addition to that, the minister will see that the manufacturers engaged in the industry will be supplied with a copy of the regulations.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
That is a very reasonable suggestion. We will see that each manufacturer gets a copy, especially as so few are engaged in the trade.
On section 8-proof by certificate:

That is very wide. I
am anxious to support the statement of the hon. gentleman who is now leading the Opposition with respect to legislation by regulations. We had the same subject up a few moments ago from the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Burrell), but I did not care to make objection then, because I understand he is not of the legal profession. I wish to bring the matter up now because my hon. friend the Minister
of Labour, who has charge of this Bill, is a lawyer of practice and experience, and eminent in his profession. As a practitioner myself I desire to point out how extremely awkward it is for a practitioner to know that there is a body of law in the country that is not to be found in any statute. It is not at all improbable that questions arising under this law may come into court some day. As a lawyer you are . expected to go to the statute and find the law, but you are placed in a very awkward position by reason of the fact that the law is not in the statute. The law is in the form of regulations, Orders in Council, and that sort of thing, and you are unable to advise on the subject until you put yourself in possession of these regulations, which you cannot get from law books, which you cannot buy from people dealing in law books, and unless you are careful in looking into the Canada Gazette and compiling these regulations it is impossible for the lawyer to keep himself in touch with them. I would recommend the Minister of Labour, and any other hon. gentleman who is bringing legislation before this House, as a matter of general principle, to try as much as possible to put their legislation in the Bill itself. Then we have it in the Act of this Parliament. I cannot see why it is easier to make regulations than an Act of Parliament. We are here as a body to make laws and the draughtsman who is going to draught regulations upon the authority of a Bill will find it just as easy to draught them in the shape of a section of the Bill and put them into the Bill itself. I make this suggestion, not only to facilitate the work of the profession to which I belong, but in the interest of the public itself, so that everybody will know what the law is without waiting to find out what has been done by regulation. It may be said that it is always easy to make a regulation on short notice, that matters will arise that cannot be foreseen and that it is necessary to make the regulation. That is the only excuse I can see for a regulation at all. But when Parliament meets once a year it cannot be a matter of very great hardship to wait from one Parliament to another in order to make any amendment that is necessary. I do not suppose I can switch the Minister of Labour from any well defined idea he has about this Bill, but I wish to put myself on record as protesting against making laws by regulations when these regulations should be in the Act itself.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
I sympathize very fully with my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie), who.

has just taken his seat. I have no doubt he has experienced, as I have many times, the inconvenience of, for instance, having to look up by-laws passed by various municipal councils. In the province of Ontario, under our Municipal Act, municipal councils are given power to pass by-laws on almost every conceivable subject and I have often experienced inconvenience in this regard. When you wanted to find out what a law really was you would have perhaps to write out to the municipality and get copies of the by-laws that it had passed. But that is a somewhat different matter from this. It would be difficult to avoid that in reference to municipal by-laws. You can go into details more readily in drawing up regulations than in passing a statute. In almost every department we have regulations. In the Interior Department they have extensive land and grazing regulations and in almost every department of the Government you will find statutes conferring upon Council the power to make regulations, and providing that these regulations shall have the same force as if they were embodied in the statute. I cannot conceive of any other reason for the authorization of these regulations than that they are very extensive, that they go into details and that it would perhaps Ibe very inconvenient to have these details enumerated in the statute. I assume these are the reasons why power is given to make these regulations and why they have the same effect as if they formed a part of the statute. My hon. friend will have noticed the power given to inspectors under certain sections of this Act. I suppose it will be necessary to have regulations directing the inspectors and going into detail as to the discharge of their duties and it might be inconvenient to spread these out on the statute. I quite sympathize with my hon. friend, as I have suffered in actual practice, as I have no doubt he has, but it is rather impracticable,
I am afraid, to get it all into the statute.
On section 11-penalty, not exceeding $500 and costs, for violation of the Act:
There is no minimum penalty in this Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
No; that is left to
the magistrate.

It is a very high
power.
On section 12-venue of proceedings:

I presume the object of this section is, that a person who might be

guilty in one province, having gone to. another province, may be prosecuted for a violation of this Act in the province in which he is located.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext: Yes.

Before the Bill is
reported, would the minister give us his impression as to how this will affect the price of matches P I have heard it said that this may create a monopoly in the manufacture of matches, and by increasing the price to a considerable extent work a hardship upon the consumers. No doubt the minister has taken this into consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
The only extra cost
involved in using sesqui-sulphide instead of white phosphorus, would be from the fact that greater skill will be required in mixing the materials. I have had communication with match manufacturers, and the maximum increase in cost was placed by them at five per cent. It is not a matter of any consequence.
Bill reported, and read the third time.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
speechtext:
The title of the Bill on the Order Paper is: 'To prohibit the manufacture and importation of matches '; I wish to have the title amended so as to read:
' To prohibit the manufacture, importation and sale of matches.'
Motion agreed to and title amended by adding the words, ' and sale.'

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext: On motion of Right Hon. R. L. Borden (Prime Minister), Bill No. 84, to amend the Export Act, was read the second time, and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The resolution on which this Bill is founded originally provided for regulations prohibiting the exportation of petroleum procured on Dominion lands. The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) pointed out that this should be in somewhat wider terms, and the resolution was accordingly amended, and the Bill drawn on the resolution in its amended form.

Do I understand this
applies only to Dominion lands f

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is general in its terms now, because of the suggestion which emanated from the hon. member for Guysborough, and which was agreed to.

The leader of the Opposition raised a point as to the propriety of stating in the Act the conditions under [DOT]which the authority, as given, would be exercised. I made some observations along the same line myself. This industry in the western provinces is in an experimental or exploratory stage. It is necessary to attract capital, and my feeling is that by passing this Bill in its present form, we would leave capital, which might be induced to invest, under an unspecified danger, which I think will have a detrimental effect.
I see no reason why the object of the Government would not be as well attained, as the Premier stated on a former occasion, by specific indication in the Bill of the conditions under which the authority would be exercised. I would urge very strongly that that be fully considered by the Government, even if it were necessary to hold the Bill over for another day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I would certainly not desire to press the Bill with undue haste, and I would be anxious to accept any modification which would preserve the object [DOT]and at the same time would not deter the investment of capital. I do not know whether my hon. friend from Edmonton has looked over the amended regulations -which have been laid upon the table of the House.
No, I did not happen to see them.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My recollection

.and I am speaking without the acquaintance of the subject possessed by the Minister of the Interior-is that the matter was brought to the attention of the Minister of the Interior during the past year on many occasions by .persons who were prepared to invest very large amounts of capital in oil production in the West, and who thought that it offered a very promising field for investment. The regulations as they formerly existed were not conducive to the investment of capital. Certain reasons were assigned, the details of which I could not give; the only thing I remember about them is that they impressed me .at the time. It was strongly urged that the regulations with regard to the production of oil had been originally prepared, by merely copying, from regulations with regard to the production of minerals of various kinds, and that the industry of oil production differed in several essential features from the industries alluded to. They pointed out that the regulations in various parts of the world where this
industry has been a success have been essentially different from those in force here. It was very largely for these reasons,
I think, that the Minister of the Interior made these amendments. At the same time, it was represented to us that, for certain reasons. which were alluded to and which it is not necessary for me	to dwell upon	at the
present moment, it might be important for us to keep oil within the country for purposes of defence; and so the resolution was introduced in the first instance purely with regard to Dominion lands and in connection with what had been set out in the first instance in the regulations themselves in that regard. The law officers of the Crown, however, advised that the Minister of the Interior had no power to make such regulations. Therefore the Minister of the Interior, after communicating with the Minister of Customs had the last mentioned minister bring in this resolution to accomplish the purpose which could not be accomplished in the regulations that had been framed in the Department of the Interior.
I would be very glad indeed if my hon. friend from Edmonton, who has had experience in these matters, and who was for a number of years at the head of the department, would look over those regulations and confer with the Minister of the Interior with regard to this particular-feature, because we are anxious to have the best knowledge and experience available in this House brought to bear upon the proposal, and to put this legislation in such form as will secure a certain purpose which has been alluded to and at the same time will not in any way deter the invest-men of capital.

I certainly agree with the object of the Bill. I would like to know from the hon. gentleman two things: first,, if similar measures will be adopted in the other overseas dominions, and second, in case the prohibition of exportation takes place, if the owners of the wells will be compensated.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The last consideration
was a little under discussion when the resolution upon this Bill was before the committee. The idea was expressed at that time by myself that it would be impossible to enforce such a prohibition without due compensation.

It is a special contingency not likely to happen very often, and

the Government would certainly take that fact into consideration.

I would like this to be borne in mind, that, in the ordinary event of changes in rates of duty, it is not held in this or any other country that people affected by such changes are entitled to compensation. It would be idle to lay down a proposal of that kind. This is a proposal, however, to prohibit absolutely for a national purpose. It would seem to me that it differs in that respect from the principle to which I have alluded just now.
So far as the other part of my hon. friend's inquiry is concerned, I am not sure as to the present existence of any regulations of this kind elsewhere in the empire; but I am quite sure that representations such as have been made to the Government have been made elsewhere, and I have no doubt that they will have the same result.
Progress reported.

The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.

speechtext: The House in Committee on Bill No. 73, respecting the Canadian Northern Railway Company.-Mr. Currie. Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
In reading this Bill over rather hurriedly, I gather that it merely authorizes a different method of attaching the signatures to securities issued.
Yes.
Insurance companies and all sorts of companies do the same at the present time.

The explanation given to the Railway Committee was that in case of securing capital in England, lenders are accustomed to the officers named in the Bill signing. The company wish that in the case of the issue of bonds or debentures, notwithstanding what is in the Railway Act, they

may be signed by the officers named in this Bill. The Bill passed the Railway Committee exactly as presented. I may add that the new consolidated Railway Act introduced in the Senate is the same as this, except that this Bill provides that these securities may be signed by the 'Assistant Local Secretary ' of the Company. The description in the new proposed railway law is ' Secretary or Assistant or Local Secretary.' speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The House resumed in Committee of Supply, Mr. Blondin in the Chair.
Miscellaneous-Expenses under the Canada Temperance Act, $5,000.
Will the hon. Secretary of State (Mr. Coderre) please explain the increase of $4,000 in this item?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: This is to meet the cost of elections under the Act. There is a great deal of interest in the Act and a considerable amount for elections will be necessary. Elections have taken place this year in Peel, Welland and Huron counties, and the department has under its consideration petitions from Algoma, Sudbury, Parry Sound, Muskoka and Niagara Falls.

Have there been any
elections in Nova Scotia?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Not this year.

In Ontario we have
what is called the local option law, which relates to townships, villages, towns and cities, while the Canada Temperance Act relates to counties. In some cases in Ontario, as I understand the situation, where the local option law may possibly not carry in one of the smaller municipalities, the temperance people are going back to the Canada Temperance Act, under which a vote for the entire county is taken, and the Act may be carried over the vote in the local town. In Ontario we have what is known as the three-fifth clause, under which the local option law requires a three-fifth vote, but under the Canadian Temperance Act only a plain majority is necessary to secure application of the law. I imagine my hon. friend will find the expense increasing during the next ten or fifteen years instead of decreasing. No doubt the temperance

people will.take advantage of the Canadian Temperance Act, and drop the local option on account of that handicap.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I believe my hon. friend is right; if I am well informed the Scott Act has been invoked only within the last few years. Before that, the temperance people used to make their petitions under the Local Option Act. I do not know why they have changed their minds, unless they believe that in this way it is easier for them to reach their aim, which is, of course, temperance. The reason why the item is larger this year than it has been in the past is because we expect that some elections will take place under the Federal Act.
Under what conditions would elections under the 'Canadian Temperance Act be held in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, where there is territory not organized into municipalities?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Some parts of the counties which I have already mentioned- Algoma, Sudbury, Parry Sound	and
Muskoka-were unorganized, and a special
list had to be prepared to meet the purposes of the Temperance Act. I believe the same thing would have to be done in those unorganized parts of Saskatchewan	and
Alberta to which my hon. friend has referred.
There are no counties in those two provinces; would the municipalities in Saskatchewan and Alberta be considered as counties under the Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: According to the law, the election takes place on the list in force at the time the petition is filed with the Secretary of State. In those unorganized parts of a county or riding there is, of course, no list available, and a special list for the purposes of the Act is made.

I understand from the minister that in the cases which have occurred in Ontario, a part of the territory in which the vote was taken was organized and a part of it was not. Would the Act cover a case where no part of the territory in which it was proposed to make the vote applicable had been organized, and, if so, at whose discretion or on whose decision would the boundaries of the district be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
If those portions of the provinces of Saskatchewan or Alberta
which the temperance people wish to bring under the Act are not organized, the same principle which it is found necessary to apply to the unorganized parts of those counties which I have mentioned should apply to them. As soon as the petitions reach the Department of the Secretary of State instructions are given to the judges to prepare the list. In such cases the list which is used is the one which is used for the purposes of a general election.

Supposing the population of a certain area of the province of Alberta, unorganized municipally, desires to have the Canadian Temperance Act applied, would the petitioners define the boundaries of the territory to which they desired the Act to apply, or would that be subject to the decision of the minister or of the judges?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I believe I am unable to answer that question.

I do not want to be understood to be asking this merely through curiosity; the condition I have stated does prevail in those provinces. There is a strong temperance sentiment; the people have been dissatisfied with the success they have achieved so far ' in attempting to secure the application of temperance enactment. I should like to be able to say definitely what the condition is under this law, which has not yet been tried in those provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not know of any case in point, and I cannot give the hon. gentleman an answer.

It is proposed to submit the Canada Temperance Act to the constituency which I have the honour to represent, a part of which is under what is known as the local option law, and a part under the Canada Temperance Act, in case the Canada Temperance Act should carry. What I want to know is whether local option would still be in force in that portion of the country, or whether the Canada Temperance Act would wipe out local option in the district altogether. The two laws are not on all fours; what would be a misdemeanor under one Act might not be under the other. I would like to get an opinion on that from the Department of Justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I wish the Minister
of Justice were here, as I cannot speak definitely on that point. I think, however,

that if the Canada Temperance Act were enforced in the whole country it would wipe out local option in all portions of the country. I must get an opinion from the Department of Justice on that point.
This is a matter of vital importance to the people I represent, and I would like to get the opinion of the Department of Justice.

I think the law is pretty
well understood in Ontario. For instance, if four municipalities in a county are under local option, and next month the Canada Temperance Act is carried in the whole county, the whole county comes under the Canada Temperance Act, and local option disappears.

I am not so sure of that. My hon. friend and myself are farmer lawyers. The question raised by the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Wright) is some question, for this reason: to carry local option in a municipality in Ontario a three-fifths vote is necessary, and to repeal local option in Ontario there has to be a a three-fifths vote, and the question is, can a majority vote repeal an Act that must be repealed by a three-fifths vote? That is a question that has not, I think, been decided yet. I am not so sure that the carrying of the Canada Temperance	Act	would affect	localoption at	all.	Suppose the	Canada Temperance Act were tried in a county and failed to carry, it is evident that' that would not interfere with the local option law in force in any municipality- at least, I think it is evident. On the other hand, if the Canada Temperance Act carried, would it override the local option law? So far as the results for the time being are concerned, it would make no difference; but when it comes to repealing the Canada Temperance Act, only a majority vote is required, while a three-fifths vote is necessary to repeal local option. It is quite a large question, and it is of interest to us in the province of Ontario to know just how the Canada Temperance Act stands, legally, in regard to local option.
Is the hon. gentleman prepared to say what steps have to be taken in order to try to pass the Canada Temperance Act in a county as a whole?
A petition is necessary, but I forget just what percentage of electors have to sign it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Twenty-five per cent of the electors.

That might have to be qualified. In a fully organized county it might be twenty-five per cent, but I do not know that that would apply to counties or districts a portion of whose territory is-unorganized.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not know whether the department's decision is right or wrong, but the first petition sent to the department was signed by only twenty-five per cent of the electors whose domicile was in the organized parts of the county. This election has been postponed to give time for a list to be prepared of the electors in the unorganized parts of the riding, and not until twenty-five per cent of the electors on the new list have signed the petition will the department act.

I do not know whether I understand the situation rightly, but it has been put before me like this: Those who get up a petition have to get twenty-five per cent of all the electors, organized and unorganized, but they are only allowed to count those voters who are in the organized districts.

Perhaps my hon. friend will get us an opinion on the question 1 raised. It is of very great importance to us in Ontario to know just what is the status of the municipalities and counties on this question.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not know in what form and when I could bring that opinion before the House as my Estimates may go through to-night.
Maybe not; we might keep one item in order to get an opinion.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I will get an opinion to-morrow if I can.

In regard to the question raised by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), in my opinion it is an impossibility to bring the Canada Temperance Act into force in Alberta and Saskatchewan under the present Act. I just want to bring this to the attention of the minister, as a case might arise and he would not have the necessary legislation. Section 2 provides for bringing it into force in British Columbia, but at the time that was passed there was no province of Alberta and no province of Saskatchewan. There was some provision for unorganized territories such as the

Northwest territories are at the present time, but I do not think that any amendment has been made to the Act in regard to the two new provinces. If it ever becomes necessary to introduce the Act in those provinces, the minister may have some trouble.

If after examination the minister decides that there is not sufficient authority in the Act at the present time to bring it into force in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, I would suggest to him that such amendments be made as would be necessary to put those provinces on an equality with the rest of the Dominion so far as the possibility of the enforcement of the Act is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I will do that.
Expenses under the Naturalization Act, $6,000.

This item is a very important one to 'this extent, that for some years there have been negotiations carried on between the Government of Canada and the British Government as to having a uniform naturalization law. I may not use the proper legal phrase in expressing my views, but as far as I understand the situation as it has been for years, a person coming to Canada and wishing to be naturalized may -be naturalized as far as Canada is concerned, but the minute he would go to another portion of the British Empire he would not be a British subject in the full sense of the term. He would be a British subject as far as being a Canadian is concerned, but the naturalization law which has been in existence in Canada would not create him a British subject throughout the empire. I think that the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Agriculture in the late Government discussed that suo-ject at length with the British authorities and that an agreement was arrived at by which a law would -be introduced that would obviate the difficulty. I think that the hon. Minister of Justice has had the matter in hand and that he has made some progress. Has the progress been sufficient up to the present date to enable us to say that hereafter the naturalization of an individual in Canada makes him a British subject throughout the empire? It is very desirable that he should be so considered. An immigrant from a foreign land comes to Canada. We only impress upon him the fact that he is a Canadian-it is limited to that practically-while the desire of all Canadians is that he should also be regarded as a British subject wherever he goes because to him it means a great deal to be a British subject away from home as well as at home and sometimes it would be a great protection to him. That matter has been under the consideration of the present Government and of the British Government and I would like to get some information from -the minister as to what progress has been made.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
This question was
brought before the Imperial Conference two years ago. I know that, generally speaking, we are unanimous in the view that in such a case as that which has been cited by my hon. friend (Mr. Graham), a Canadian should be a British subject the world over. I could not say more now than that which was said lately by my hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty). I know that certain correspondence has taken place between the imperial authorities and the Department of Justice with a view to coming to a final settlement upon this point in a sense favourable to the opinion which has been expressed by my hon. friend; but I do not know of anything else in connection with the matter.

It struck me that an
agreement had been practically arrived at by which there would be concurrent legislation in the British Parliament and in the Parliament of Canada. It was merely to get some definite information if I could concerning it that I put the question to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I do not think the Minister of Justice has received the good news that a final settlement has been reached.

I was not in and did not hear all that was said by the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham). This is a question in which I have felt a good deal of interest, but I do not think it is fair that we should pass legislation to make a man a British subject throughout the whole British Empire. I think that sometimes we are rather lax in our laws regarding naturalization. I understand that in the West a year's residence -qualifies a man for naturalization. Is that correct?
No.

Then, I am mistaken. I thought that was the case and if it was I did not think that we would have any reason to claim that a man should be declared to be a British subject on a short

residence of that kind when in other parts of tne British Empire perhaps a longer residence would be required. I think it proper that each country should deal with a matter of this kind according to its own opinion. I would not urge that we should declare a man to be a British subject the empire over simply because conditions which might be less onerous might suit our purposes very well. I do not think we would be justified in asking other portions of the Britisn Empire to accede to our request. I do not exactly share the view which was thrown out by the hon. member for South Renfrew.
I am afraid that my hon. friend has been led into error by the fact, as stated by himself, that he was not in when I was speaking.
Possibly.

The object of the British and Canadian authorities, as well as those of other overseas dominions, was to arrive at a basis for uniform legislation so that a man naturalized in any part of the British Empire would be a British subject where-ever he went. But it is not so easy to do that as it might appear on the surface. The governments of the overseas dominions and the Imperial authorities have been discussing it for some years and I had rather thought that they had arrived at a solution by whch we could have uniform legislation that would apply to all the overseas dominions as well as to Great Britain.

Would my hon.
friend be perfectly willing that the Parliament of South Africa should declare that a man should become a naturalized citizen of the Dominion of Canada? I think we should reserve that power to ourselves. We do not know what they might do in other parts of the British Empire; they might perhaps do something not at all satisfactory to us. I would rather retain the power within ourselves to say that a man should be,' or that he should not be, a British subject.

Well, then, we do not
make him a British subject altogether ; we only make him a piece of one.
We only make him a Canadian subject.
That is all.

I should like to call the attention of the Secretary of State to what

seems to me to be a hardship inflicted upon people who make application for naturalization. I have not taken the trouble to look into the Act, but in our part of the country, if you get into court to get a person naturalized and give the ordinary notice, before the certificate is issued, the clerk, if it is in the county court, or the prothonotary, if in the Supreme Court, makes it necessary for the applicant to appear in his office to sign some documents and get his certificate. I suppose this is a uniform practice all 'over Canada and no doubt it is done under the Naturalization Act. But it is a great hardship. The application is always made in the shire town of the county and the applicant may reside one hundred and fifty miles away from the shire town. If the law is put into effect, as it has been in our county of South Cape Breton, it will necessitate the applicant paying out $2 or $3 for transportation, in addition to the loss of a day, .in order to. oome into the shire town to get his naturalization certificate. I would ask the Secretary of State to bring this matter to the attention of the Minister of Justice who may be able to do something to make it easier for these people. In my part of the country, they force us to bring the applicants to the shire town after the certificate has been granted, and I do not see the necessity for that.

What is this money
for?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
There is a semi-annual return of the persons naturalized throughout the Dominion, furnished by some 400 officers at various ports, and this is to pay their fees, which are fixed by Order in Council.
For supply of Canadian publications to library of High Commissioner's office, $500.
There is no High Commissioner, and I think we ought to be told who is going to read this literature.
The High Commissioner.
Who is he?
He may be the member for South Renfrew.

No chance, under present conditions. The position of High Commissioner for Canada in London is a very important one, and it ought not to be left longer vacant. It may be that there is a surplus of men longing to sacrifice themselves in that office, particularly as the Government press announces that the sal-

ary Is to be raised to $30,000 a year. The Government would have been well advised, I think, not t-o have announced that until the appointment had been made, because it only multiplies their troubles. There are gentlemen who would be likely to accept the office at $30,000 per annum who perhaps could not see their way clear to take it at the modest sum of $20,000. Many rumours are rife as to who is to be High Commissioner, and now that we are undertaking to supply him with literature, it becomes a question as to whether we should supply reading material for a man who is not on the job. My modest business has been running a newspaper foT a number of years, and the difficulty I had was to get pay from actual subscribers.
You could always get cord wood.

Yes, but short length
usually. We on this side of the House will have nothing to say as to who should be appointed to that honourable and important position, but we can at least urge, with some degree of reasonableness, that the vacancy should no longer be allowed to exist.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Have you any suggestion to make?

If we need a High Commissioner in London, as'we do, we need him all the time, and if there be men in Canada, as there are many, who are able to fill this position, they are available now just as much as they will be available three months hence. In all seriousness, I think the Government should give us some idea as to who the High Commissioner is to be. The names of several members of the present Government have got into the public mind, through an aperture created by some person, and we ought to know if the present array of Ministers is to be depleted. If the next High Commissioner is to be a member of the Government, why not say so at once and allay the lingering suspense and fears of a number of aspirants who are on the outside. I think myself that some of the present ministers might be spared without doing any serious injury to the ship of state. There are two of the ministers present, and perhaps they can tell us, without breaking faith with their colleagues, and without creating any jealousy between them, who, in their opinion, should be High Commissioner; of course, they need not mention their own names. If a member of the Government is to become High Corn-112
missioner, it should be announced now, so that the Prime Minister may have ample time to look around him for a substitute. For example, if it is to be the Minister of Public Works, he might get a gentleman from Calgary to succeed him. I would not say that he would be my selection, but he would fill the vacancy in the Government without having a gentleman move from Manitoba to Saskatchewan to get a constituency there, as has been suggested. If the Minister of Militia is to be High Commissioner, I can see two or three prospective Ministers of Militia from the province of Ontario, who would be willing to take the portfolio and relieve the situation.
What would you do with the others who would be disappointed?
They would have to wait until some other member of the Government got an office of emolument. Suppose the next High Commissioner should be a member of the Government from Nova Scotia.
Never.

Well, it has been intimated that the position might be filled by a prominent member of the Government from Nova Scotia, and if that be so we ought to know it at once, because I think I could find a Conservative from Nova Scotia who would be willing to take office in his place.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: This money is voted for the next fiscal year, which starts only on the first of April next.
April fool.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: We will have plenty of time in the interim to make the appointment.
Will the hon. gentleman promise that the appointment will be made before the first of April?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I cannot swear to that, but I can say that the Government will do its utmost to make a speedy and a good appointment.
You had better leave out the word ' speedy.'

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I remember that an
appointment made by the Conservative Government some years ago was considered to be so good that, when the Liberal party came into power, they thought they



could no do better than keep the appointee in his position.

And they did not appoint a commission to investigate that appointtee?
Mr.	CODERRE:	I think	members	on
both sides of the House and the general public will certainly find that we shall appoint a good successor to the late lamented Lord Strathcona.
Mr.	GRAHAM:	Which	minister	will
it be ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I know some ministers who would be good successors to Lord Strathcona, but I do not know any who have expressed a desire to go to London.
Mr.	LEMIEUX:	The Government	can
appoint a successor to Lord Strathcona, but they can appoint no one to replace him. He was accredit not only to Canada but to the whole of the British Empire.
There is another	point to	be
9 p.m. considered in regard to this vote to add to the library of the High Commissioner's office. My hon. friend has not gone to London since he has been made a minister of the Crown; but some day he will go there and will see that the office of the High Commissioner of Canada is far too congested. It is crowded with employees, with newspapers, blue books, and the usual library containing books of general information about Canada. To all those who have been at that office, it is only too obvious that it is out of date and certainly not in keeping with the constant growth of Canada's business in Great Britain.
In regard to this question of a new office in London, my hon. friend is aware that a movement is on foot to provide our country with a suitable building. Some years ago it was a debatable question whether the office should not be removed from Victoria street, where it now is, to the neighbourhood of Charing Cross; and then, as the site was found a little expensive, the question remained in abeyance until of late our former Governor General, Lord Grey, took up the matter and was appointed president of a committee in London which had for its special object to secure a site known as the Aldwych site where the various dominions and notably Canada would erect a building. Practically all the members of this House have received plans and photographic views of that site, also resolutions, and expressions of opinion from the press of the various overseas dofMr. Coderre.]
minions, all favourable to the site selected by Lord Grey and his associates. Some weeks ago I asked the Prime Minister if any decision had been arrived at. He replied that no decision has yet been made by Council. Is my hon. friend in a position to say whether the matter has been considered by the Government, and when we are likely to know whether or not a new site will be provided in London for Canada? The late Lord Strathcona was opposed to a new building or site, I suppose, because, being quite an old man, he did not care to change his habits. He had been accustomed for the last eighteen years to go to 19 Victoria street to transact business there, and he was quite satisfied with his own office. I appeal to my hon. friend the Postmaster General, who has been to Great Britain last year on an official mission, to say whether or not the Canadian offices in London are adequate for the business of Canada there. You have in one row of buildings the offices * of New Zealand, I believe also those of South Africa, and those of one of the smaller colonies next to the offices of Canada. That the smaller colonies may be satisfied with such small offices is no reason why the greater dominions should be satisfied with them. They are not in the central part of London, and I think we are entitled to something more ornamental than what we have in Victoria street. The Canadian immigration office, although in appearance not monumental, yet is very centrally situated near the statue of Charles I. on Charing Cross; and at night, when the illumination of the office advertising Canada is seen, it is a striking advertisement for our country. I think the Canadian office proper ought to be at some similar point. I do not say that we should take the Aldwych site, although for my part I would certainly vote quite a large amount of money to secure for Canada in London, the nerve centre of the empire, the best site available. Delegates were sent here a few weeks ago to interview the Government. Perhaps my hon. friend, without breaking any great secret, will be able to tell us whether Canada will have a respectable office in London or not.
As regards the appointment of a High Commissioner, as I stated a moment ago, you can appoint a successor to Lord Strathcona, but you will hardly find any one to replace him. It is well known that for years Lord Strathcona never drew his salary; or, if he drew it, he gave it away for charitable purposes. The salary as it is now in the Estimates, is certainly not adequate to the position just as

the salary which we paid some years ago to our commissioner in Paris was not adequate to that position. You do not pay the salary of the man only, you must pay something for the office also. The man who is our commissioner in London or in Paris must spend some money to represent his country, and if you give him only a paltry sum, our country will thereby suffer. I learned with great pleasure that the Government had increased the salary of our commissioner in Paris. It is .admitted that the Hon. Mr. Roy is doing his best to represent our country worthily in that great city of Paris. In London, the centre of the empire, and one might say the centre of the world, the representative of Canada, the premier colony of the empire, surely should be adequately paid. I do not know whom the Government intend to appoint to that position. Several names have been mentioned. Not very long ago there was quite a campaign in favour of Lord Mount-stephen. I do not know whether he would be willing to accept the position, but certainly, if he could be induced to accept it, no better Canadian could be given the appointment. But he is rather old, and 1 do not suppose he cares for the office. The best man must be selected, and you' must pay him accordingly. Whoever is selected by the Government, I am sure, will be a creditable representative, for one who has [DOT]travelled on the other side knows full well that the High Commissioner for Canada occupies a very exalted position. At the time of the Coronation our commissioner was given by His Majesty the King the rank of an ambassador. Therefore, the representative of Canada is a man highly considered, not in Great Britain only, but throughout Europe. The appointment must go to the best man, and an adequate salary must be provided.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
In what my hon. friend from Rouville (Mr. Lemieux) has said about Lord Strathcona, I heartily concur. Lord Strathcona rendered great service to Canada, and, as my hon. friend has said, he will not easily be replaced. He was a national figure; he represented this country in London for many years, not only to his own credit but to the credit and benefit of the country. Whoever is appointed to succeed him will find it difficult to fill his place. I hope we shall be able to find in Canada a suitable' man. If we listen to the suggestion of the hon.
member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), we shall certainly find somebody who will consent to accept the post. One of the difficulties is that the salary which the representative of Canada receives is, as my hon. friend from Rouville said, very small. Of course, in the case of Lord Strathcona, that fact had no importance whatever; he was so wealthy and so generous in spending his money for so many good purposes, including lavish expenditures in the interests of Canada. I hope that before long, as the office has to be filled and creditably filled, the Government will be in a position to make an announcement on the subject.
As to the Canadian office in London, I think that the members on both sides agree that our present offices are not all that they should be. As the hon. member for Rouville has said, they are small, and perhaps they are not on the street most-frequented by people who would have an interest in the affairs that centre in that office. As to the Aldwych site, of course that is a very big contract. Probably the House and the country are not aware that if we were to acquire that site from the Corporation of London under the option which Lord Grey has, and to put up a building under the plans of which the hon. member for Rouville spoke, the total expenditure would be not less than 114,000,000.
For Canada?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
The total. But in this respect one thing is to be mentioned. Of course the idea which the delegates had in mind when they came here recently and were heard by the members of the Government, was that several of the overseas dominions might join in order to share the expense to a certain extent. But several of the overseas dominions have already provided sites for themselves, and, moreover, as in the case of Australia, have provided themselves with buildings; the Australian building is very suitably located and very creditable; and it is out of the question that Australia would join and share the expense of the Aldwych site. It has been suggested that the different provinces of Canada might join and have their offices in the same building. 1 am not in a position to say whether the provinces would accept that idea or not. As a matter of fact, the several provinces now have offices in London, some of them very fine offices. The province of Ontario is well housed, and the office of the province of Quebec,

in Kingsway, is so well located and so fine that we do not know that the provincial government would consent to undertake so large an expenditure as its share in moving to the Aldwych site would represent. So, the question is a big one, a very big one indeed; and while the Government is desirous of having as good a location as possible, it has not been decided, so far, that the Aldwych site will be accepted. At the same time, the mind of the Government is moving in the direction of having some suitable quarters on a suitable site. We all agree that our offices in London ought to be well situated. And I concur in what my hon. friend from Rouville said about our immigration office.
It has been hoped that we might possibly 'get a property on Trafalgar Square, but legal conditions and other circumstances make it difficult to do so. However, we are turning our attention in that direction, and we hope to be able to accomplish something. I am happy to join- in what the hon. member for Rouville has said about our representative in Paris. In that regard I think we have improved matters very much. Formerly the representative of Canada in Paris was also the, representative of the province of Quebec, and with the two salaries he received, one voted by this Parliament and one by the Legislature of the province of Quebec, the amount was not as much as it is to-day. Realizing the great importance of having a creditable office in Paris, such as we now have in the Boulevard des Capucins, we have asked the province of Quebec to appoint its own representative, having reached the conclusion that it is better for the federal Government to have a representative of its own. We have given Mr. Roy what might be called a decent salary and we are voting him besides some $3,500 in order to give him enough to do honour and credit to this country. Mr. Roy was appointed by the late Government. I saw his work when I was in Paris, and I have heard very many good things about him; consequently we ' have not only retained his services but have bettered his position as well. Mr. Roy has devoted all his energies to his work, and is a creditable representative of Canada in Paris. I am happy to say, to use a well-known expression, that he has made good. If in London we can accomplish something along the same line, and have in one of the great thoroughfares *of that city such an office as we have on the Boulevard des Capucins in Paris, the sooner it can be done the better for this country.
I Mr. Pelletier.]
Does Earl Grey's option include an outright title to the property, or simply an emphyteutic lease?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Fee simple.

The important question is not so much the selection of a Canadian palace in the heart of the empire as it is the securing of the best possible representative for our country, who will assume his duties more from a business than from a social point of view. I would like to see a native Canadian in that office, a man born in Canada-no matter in what part of it-a man with all the energy and vigour of youth, and, most important of all, a man thoroughly acquainted with our Dominion, its resources and its needs. We want a man in London not merely to entertain Canadians who happen to go there, but a man who knows Canada's requirements, who is acquainted with her trade and its development, and who can help to build it up; who will assist in getting the best class of immigration from Europe, and who will look at the office and the fulfilment of the duties it involves from a business point of view. I am not passing the slightest criticism on any previous holder of that eminent office, and I am not saying that holders of the office have been sufficiently remunerated in the past; but it is not so much a question of the remuneration as it is a matter of the office being held by a man who will look at it from the Canadian businesslike point of view. The man who represents Canada in London should, to my mind, be eminently acquainted with financial conditions; he ought to know how to aid Canada in getting what she most needs from the mother country and from Europe, that is, capital. A man competent to do these things is the kind of man who should be sought, and I think he can be found among the natives of Canada.

Much as I hesitate to differ from the hon. gentleman, allow me to protest, as a native Canadian, against the claim that he has made-that men who are not native Canadians are not qualified to represent this country.
I did not say that.

I understood the hon. gentleman to say he would like to see a native Canadian sent over to Great Britain to represent Canada. From this I infer that he means that in order that we may have a man who is thoroughly Canadian, he will have to be a Canadian of the Canadians, as it is said, and one who is

not, as I think he meant to insinuate, tainted with foreign blood.
I did not say that at all.

I have very great
respect for the hon. gentleman who has just spoken; I regard him as one of the most progressive men in Canada, but let me say that men who have come to this country from other parts of the British Empire have identified themselves in every possible way with Canada, and are just as good Canadians as exist in this country. We have in the old country men from Canada who are accepted wholly without prejudice, and who are accorded positions not with reference to their nationality, but because they are British subjects, who are loyal to the empire and faithful to their duty. The very moment you bring up the distinction at which the hon. gentleman has hinted, you will utterly break up the whole British Empire, because you accentuate or emphasize birth or nationality, and this we should not be too anxious to emphasize.
Does my hon. friend suggest that the hon. member for South York (Mr. Maclean) would break up the British Empire?

I do not suggest that he wishes to do so; I do not suggest that other gentlemen in this House wish to do so, but I do suggest that if the course they pursue is followed, they will break it up. I speak with some feeling in this matter, for many years ago, when I had,. perhaps, a little less sense than I have now, I w'ent into this matter and, if I may be forgiven, I wrote a little book called, ' Canadians in the Imperial Service.'
I went over Canada and I went over the old country, looking the whole matter up, and I found a bond of sympathy between the men who are ready to serve the empire. They did not ask whether they were Canadians, or Englishmen. I found Canadians living in London wholly adopted by the English people and I find English people in Canada wholly adopted by Canadians, and I trust there never will be, especially at this time when we are seeking to acquire equality of naturalization, any attempt to differentiate between different sections and different nations. Let my hon. friend from Rouville remember that if we begin that sort of thing it might be bad for the French in Canada. If we are going to start that sort of thing there will be no welding of the nations. , We who are	anxious-as	English-speaking
Canadians-to take	to our inmost
heart our French	compatriots, are
forbidden by that doctrine to do so. Who will be the Canadians in this country, who will be the British subjects, if we are going to adopt doctrines like that? The people here will be Canadians and Australians will be Australians. The next thing, we shall have British Columbians howling that they belong to British Columbia only, and similarly with the middle West. We have had enough of that already; we must give up that idea. I am speaking perhaps hastily, because this matter has been flashed upon me, but I know I am right. It is a very serious question that is being broached, and I think a very wrong one.
Public archives, $48,500.
This is one of the items I would question a decrease in, not because I do not favour economy, but because I hope there is to be no cessation of the important work tin connection with the Archives.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: There is a decrease of $4,500. Last year there were a few outstanding accounts in England which had to be paid. This year we have no outstanding accounts and the amount required is less on that account; that is the only reason for the decrease.

I am sorry that the Government does not appreciate the importance of the work done by the Archives staff. A year ago I inquired of the Government if the time had not come when we should enlarge the building now occupied by the Archives Branch. This building was erected only a few years ago, but the work of the Archives staff has been so productive that to-day it is overcrowded. Let us retrace our steps for one moment. Some forty years ago the Archives were put under the direction of Dr. [DOT] Brymner. The Archives Branch was at that time put under control of the Department of Agriculture- why, I do not know. Dr. Brymner certainly accomplished wonders with the money and the space at his disposal. I think he was given three or four small rooms. It was during Dr. Brymner's occupancy of the position of archivist that he began the study and the copying of our historic documents, chiefly in France and England. We secured some very valuable documents. Later on, when Dr. Brymner was superannuated, the Government was fortunate enough to secure the services of a gentle

man eminent as an archivist not only in America but throughout the world; I refer to Dr. Doughty. His special fitness for the position, his great culture, and his services to the country, are well known. I believe that any government in the world would be glad to secure Dr. Doughty's services. When a document does not exist he almost invents one. He has made discoveries which have baffled every historian and archivist, but unfortunately Dr. Doughty has not sufficient assistance in his work. I am not passing judgment on any of his subordinates; I think they are all able men; but I do not think he has the requisite number around him for the splendid work he is accomplishing. The building, as I said, is quite inadequate, and I wish to call the attention of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to that point. We have erected a mint which is a credit to Canada, and I think we should have a monumental building for our archives. The present building is already full to the roof, as any one who goes there can easily realize. There is another thing: the public have recently been admitted to the museum on Sundays as well as week days, and statistics show that a great number of people availed themselves of that opportunity to visit the museum. I do not ask that the Archives Branch be kept open on Sundays, but I think the time during which the building is available to the public is not very long. The office closes at 8 o'clock in the evening and is opened at 9.30 or perhaps 10 o'clock in the morning. The student of history is not satisfied with such a short day's work, and if a limited number of students were permitted to avail themselves of these splendid collections for a longer time each day, I am quite sure they would heartily rejoice in that fact. Mr. Chairman, do you realize what a mine we have at the Archives? We have many important buildings in Ottawa; we have the Mint where we coin our gold and our silver, we have our library and we have our museum, but I dare say our most interesting building is the Archives building. Historians of the past, the Dents, the Christies, the Garneaus, the Suites, to name but a few of those who belonged to the older generation, if they had to write again the history of Canada, or one period of that history, would recast their work. They certainly deserve well for the work that they did, but had they had in then-day all the manuscripts and the original documents which have been collected of fMr. Lemieux.l
late by Dr. Doughty, it would have made the greatest difference in the world to them. Dr. Doughty, in writing a report some years ago and speaking of the importance of the archives in the preparation of any history, said:
In the course of an examination by a Select Committee of the British House of Commons many years ago, the chairman put the following question to a well known author. ' Do you think that owing to those causes a work so inaccurate as Hume's History of England, we And the currency in the present day that it did at the time it was published? ' The answer given was:	'I do not think it would. I wish
to speak with the highest respect of Robertson and Hume, two most eminent men. I have heard that the demand for their works is much diminished, and I believe the fact is so, but I think that it is to be ascribed, not to there being no demand for higher historical literature, but to these authors not having gone to the best sources from which historical truth was to be drawn: these sources were not opened to them at least not so open that they could easily consult them, and therefore I do not mean to say, they are to be blamed. Hume, I have heard, was shown the stores in the State paper office, or some other of the great record offices after he had gained a great reputation by the publication of his first volumes. He was in London, and about to continue his work, but his time was limited; he looked on the uncatalogued array of manuscripts in despair and contented himself with those printed materials which were accessible.'
Here you have the experience of Hume. Without the archives it would be the experience of every Canadian historian. The archives have changed completely the field of Canadian history. Documents of the highest importance which were not known to exist, which were not accessible to these historians, have been brought to light during the last eight or ten years. My friend, Dr. Doughty, has discovered in Mexico, in the far West, in Illinois, most invaluable collections which were supposed to be lost for one or two centuries, and which have a direct relation to the history of Canada. In the seminary of St. Sulpice in Montreal, in the seminary of Quebec, in the court house of Montreal, in the court house of Quebec, papers were buried in the dust for centuries of the utmost importance to every one who wishes to ' study the old regime in Canada, and nobody had ever thought of getting possession of these papers. I say nobody. Pardon me, the Americans had been enterprising enough to get those documents, and Dr. Doughty has found in Chicago, in Wisconsin, and in New Orleans papers which belonged to the court house in Montreal and the court house in Quebec. They had been taken by

Americans to their own country at the expense of Canada. In England, Dr. Doughty has discovered most invaluable documents-the Townshend collection, the Chatham papers, the Bagot papers, the Durham papers and the Dalhousie papers. The papers relating to the Riel state trial have been found in the Justice Department. They were about to be lost, and if Dr. Doughty had not laid his. hands on a box containing the record in that case, they would have disappeared. Some years ago he wanted to get some charts which were supposed to be shelved somewhere in the Militia Department. He was told that no such charts existed. Well, he went into the garrets of the department, and he discovered charts of the highest value, not only to Canada but to the empire itself.
These facts are not known, and yet it is well that they should be. We must help as much as possible the archivist of the Dominion in getting the necessary appropriation, first, to enlarge the building where he is now located, and, second, to increase his staff. No family in Canada can dispense wiith the archives. I dare say that there is no nation in the world to-day which can trace the genealogy of its citizens better than the Canadian nationality. As regards my fellow countrymen the French in Canada, it is well known that in view of the careful way in which the registers were kept by the clergy and the courts under the French regime, it is very easy for them to trace their ancestry. The English-speaking race, especially of the province of Ontario, will find here the titles of concession in every township. They have been discovered by Dr. Doughty, and they are in the archives building. The descendants of nearly every settler, including the United Empire Loyalists in Ontario, can find the original patents which those settlers got from the King, or his representative, at the time they settled in this country.
This is an important matter, not only for the Canadian families, but for the country at large and I am not satisfied when I see that the amount is decreased by my hon. friend the Secretary of State. I hope that this decrease only has reference to this one vote, and that there will be something in the Supplementary Estimates which will compensate for it. I may tell the committee that Dr. Doughty has also secured the correspondence of Sir John Macdonald. He has secured the papers of the De Sala-berry family, and he has been able from
that correspondence to establish some facts which heretofore have been contested. He
received considerable additions to his state documents from His Excellency Lord Grey when he was Governor General, and also from Lord Minto. That very excellent book, ' Constitutional Documents,' compiled by Mr. Shortt and Dr. Doughty, is due to the existence of the Archives. The instructions given by the home governments to the various governors of Canada, which, of course, had to remain confidential for a number of years, were recently made public and add greatly to our knowledge of the constitutional history of our country. It is of the utmost importance to students of history that they should be cognizant of such documents. I sincerely hope that the Secretary of State will give to the Archives what help he possibly can, and will induce the Minister of Public works to reconstruct the Archives building. There is no building in Canada that should be more monumental, because in it you have tne history of every Canadian family, and you have as well the papers of the nation. The people of Canada would be surprised did they know the extent of the treasures that have been accumulated during the past ten or fifteen years by the Dominion Archivist, and by some of his staff.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I can assure my hon.
[DOT]riend (Mr. Lemieux) that the interest he :akes in the Archives is not greater than he interest taken in that institution by the Government. It is a pleasure to me to in-iorm my friend that in the supplementary estimates for the coming year there will be found a sum for the extension of that building, which will make it three times as large as it is at present. I am m accord with the hon. .member when he says that the present building no longer suits the demands of the Archives Department. We have already there 13,000 old maps, most of them relating to the history of the country, and 20,000 volumes or manuscripts of all kinds. What has been said by the hon. member should be known to all Canadians who are proud of the history of their country The decrease of .$4,500 in the vote is according to the wish of the Dominion Archivist. What my hon. friend has said of Dr. Doughty, is not too much. I believe he is the right man for the position; he loves his work, and during the ten years he has been in office the number of maps and manuscripts and valuable volumes has

largely increased. Dr. Doughty reports that the officers in the Archives at present are sufficient to do the work properly. It has been a pleasure for the Government to have recently authorized the renting of offices in Montreal and Quebec, where the representatives of the Archives Department can carry on their work instead of working at home. We have in Nova Scotia, Mr. Milner, who is a well-known litterateur and historian, and he is doing splendid work. Lately we have appointed an official in Winnipeg, who will exploit the wealth of historical lore to be found in the records of the Hudson Bay Company, and which will prove a valuable addition to our history.
Have the Selkirk papers been secured?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, sixty volumes of
them are now in the Archives. There is a total sum of $109,800 voted for the Dominion Archives, and the Archivist believes it is sufficient. He has been refused nothing, and the Government have only been too pleased to do whatever was deemed necessary by the Archivist.
What Canadians are employed in Paris under the Dominion Archivist?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Messrs. Beauchesne,
Buron, and Dugas.
Who in London?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Biggar, Mr. French, and five copyists.
Is there a representative of our Archives in Washington?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: No, but we have Mr. Lanctot in California,

I would urge upon my hon. friend that, when an appointment is to be made at the Archives, he should follow the judgment of the Chief Archivist. When the Liberal party was in office we did not select, for the Archives at least, any officer unless his appointment was approved by the Chief Archivist. When we appointed an assistant to the Archivist, we selected Mr. Roy of Levis, Quebec. He was a well-known Conservative; but, as an archivist and as a student in history, he was supposed to be a leading authority in Canada. I would like my hon. friend to follow in the footsteps of his predecessors and not to impose upon Dr. Doughty any political appointment. If there is one sacred place in the departments where technical and special knowledge is re-
quired, it is in the Archives. If you impose upon the Archivist any political friend who has no special knowledge of history, you simply create chaos and confusion. Will my hon. friend give his word that he will always consult the Chief Archivist and not make him turn to despair?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: My hon. friend knows that these appointments are made on the issuing of a certificate from the Civil Service Commissioners.
This is a good old joke.
They come in under section 21.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Since I have come into office, I have followed the system in vogue. I know that in some cases Liberals have been appointed because they were deemed by Dr. Doughty to be the best qualified. My hon. friend knows Mr. Lanctot and what his political principles are. I feel that a permanent appointment should be made, because I think that he is only there temporarily. He has been sent by the Archivist to California to do special work for the Archives, and I believe that before long he will prove one of our best archivists so far as the history of Canada, at all events, is concerned. He has taken a great deal of interest in his work, and I have been only too pleased to do what I can for him. There are also young students belonging to different universities in Canada who have been helped in the same way. We do not take the trouble to go into the family records or old manuscripts to find out whether they belong to this or that party.

I know Mr. Lanctot very well, and I hope that some day'he will bfe a permanent official of that de-
10 p.m. partment. Mr. Lanctot was a *student of mine some years ago at Laval University. He took all his degrees there and even was awarded a Rhodes scholarship. When the time came to select one of the three Rhodes scholars that Canada can send every year to Oxford, it was found that the Quebec branch of Laval University was entitled to the scholarship, and young Lanctot, who belonged to the Montreal branch, missed his turn, but was promised that the following year he would be sent to Oxford. When he applied the following year to Dr. Parkin for his scholarship, he was told that he was a year too old. After that he earned his living for some time, making a little money by writing for the press; then he went to

Oxford; was admitted to the University; followed the courses there for three years- and I may say en passant that one of the noble actions of Lord Strathcona was to help that young Canadian. He is the one who introduced lacrosse at Oxford. He completed his studies at Oxford, and has now returned to Canada. He does not know whether he will take up law, journalism or history; but he is certainly well able to fill a post in the Archives building. He does not seek the office; the office is seeking him; and my hon. friend is simply doing a good action, not only in the interest of Lanctot, but of the Archives and of the country. I can assure him that he will never have a better officer than young Lanctot.
Is Mr. Lanctot a Liberal?

Yes, when the former
Administration appointed Mr. Roy, of Levis, as assistant archivist, ihe was recognized at the time as a great authority in the held of historical research; and at the same time he was well known as a prominent Conservative in the province of Quebec.
That is exactly what I said a moment ago to the hon. Secretary of State, and if there is a department from which politics should be banished, surely that is the one. Office holders under that department should be appointed on account of their qualifications and not on account of their political colour.

I would like to know from the minister who it is decides whether such or such a document and such or such a flag should be deposited in the Archives. I have gone through the Archives, I saw there the flag of Carillon, guns dating back to 1837 and a great many other things of very great interest. I wonder at times whether the Nationalists' colours is not to be found there, I mean that flag riddled with bullets.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
If it is not there, it might be of interest to know where it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
We have what is termed the Commission of Historical manuscripts, which comprises among others the hon. Mr. Chapais, legislative councillor, of Quebec; the Revd. Mr. Gosselm, of Laval University, Quebec; Mr. Colby, of McGill University, and several others, residing in various provinces of the Dominion. That commission is, as it were, the board of directors of the Archives. Mr. Doughty, the Archivist, is on the board. It meets at Ottawa several times in the year, and at such meetings, Mr. Doughty makes such recommendations as he thinks proper; he informs the board of what has been done since the previous meeting. It is that commission which acts as advisor to the archivist. In that way is the selection made in most cases of the manuscripts, which, as I stated a moment ago, number about 20,000, and also of the maps, numbering 13,000, which have been selected as having some historical value.
My hon. friend must have found highly interesting the visit he made to the Archives. Not only did he see there the old flag of Carillon, but he must also have noticed the large numbers of these manuscripts and charts.

I wish to find out from the Minister whether the statute which was passed a year or two ago, when the archivist was promoted to the rank of a deputy minister, providing that he should be allowed to enter all departments and to lay hands on all historical documents he might discover there, has been given effect to in the meantime. Has Mr. Doughty met with difficulties in securing such documents? I understand in every department there are exceedingly valuable documents which are liable to be lost or mislaid, but which the archivist has the right to have deposited in the Archives.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I may say to my hon. friend that last year a commission was organized, made up of Sir Joseph Pope, Mr. Jarvis and Dr. Doughty. The secretary of that commission was Mr. Justice Audette. That commission was appointed to go through every department, exhume any old documents which may be stored there and many of which are on the road to utter destruction. That commission has done a certain amount of work. When it is through it is expected it will submit to us a report, and I understand that will be

the proper time to decide what documents are worthy of a place in the Archives, and to obtain from the various ministers authority to transfer them to the Archives. Until that is done, I think it would not be possible to arrive at a decision.
Legislation-general-printing, printing paper and binding, $250,000.
Has this to do with the printing of the reports?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
