speechtext: This money is for the expenses of the Printing Committee of Parliament to pay for the printing and stationery they need from the Printing Bureau.
Can the hon. minister inform me whether we may have the list for the county of Jacques Cartier?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes.
I mean the latest list, not the one for the last election.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman
wants the list of last fall?

I mean the list for the coming election. The hon. minister knows that there is a new law in the province of Quebec and that we have adopted tne one-man-one-vote system. This makes a great difference for such counties as Jacques Cartier, Chambly and Vaudreui/1 .surrounding the city of Montreal. There is a large floating population in these counties who have heretofore had a right to vote and whose names are now eliminated from the lists.
1 dare say there are 5,000 persons at least who were entitled to vote in the last election in Jacques Cartier who will be eliminated by the new system. I do not wish to conceal my demand: there will be an election in the county of Jacques Cartier, and I ask the hon. Secretary of State to have the list prepared according to the last revision.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I know that when there is a vacancy, it is customary for the Clerk of the Crown in Chancery to prepare the list. If the hon. gentleman thinks it necessary for me to remind Mr. Foley of the custom. I will do it with pleasure.

I am not criticising Mr. Foley, nor do I make any request of him. 1 make my request frankly and boldly to the Minister of the Department. There is a vacancy in Jacques Cartier; we shall have an election there; the lists will be required; both of the parties will want it. I now beg to make my request on behalf of the Lib- .
erals of the county of Jacques Cartier for the list, and I desire that it shall be supplied as soon as possible. It is known that there will be an election; it is known that about one-third of the electorate at the last vote will be eliminated. Now, why not have a proper list prepared at once? Will the hon. Secretary of State tell me that he will give the necessary instructions to that effect?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Yes, I will give the
necessary instructions; and as soon as the list is ready my hon friend or any other member will be given a copy.
Are these lists printed every year, or is this a sign of an election?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
According to law, I
understand, the lists of the whole country should be prepared annually. That would mean an expenditure of $80,000. It has been the custom for years not to prepare the lists in those years in which a general election is not expected; and as we do not expect a general election this year, the lists generally have not been made. But, in a case such as that referred to by my hon. friend from Rouville, the list will be prepared as soon as possible.
The hon. gentleman will give especial instructions to Mr. Foley?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Yes.

Thank you.
Miscellaneous-plant, Printing Bureau, new, $50,000.
Will the minister please tell us just what he is going to buy, where he is going to buy it, and how he is going to buy it?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Three cylinder presses, at $3,500 each. We have been buying the Meihle presses. They are not made in this country, and we get them from Chicago.
Printing His Majesty's documents upon American presses? I cannot believe it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
We are obliged to do
so, because these presses are not made in Canada.
They are made in England.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Not the same presses.
Then there is an item for one automatic job press, composing room equipment, paper cutter, cutting machine, sewing machine, etc., total, $50,000.

The Meihle is a good
press, but there are many other good ones. The judgment of the department may be all right, but if I were buying presses I would not announce that 1 intended to buy only the Meihle, because by so doing I would shut out all competition and, besides. would have to pay whatever price was asked.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
We have been buying
some of these presses, but I do not remember having announced it to be the intention of the department to buy these particular presses from the same company. There are special reasons why these presses should be bought. I am told that a man who can work on that press can work on any other.
Distribution of parliamentary documents, $2,000.

The members of the
House are allowed four copies of the unrevised ' Hansard.' I do not know what is the experience of other hon. gentlemen, but I have demand for a great many more than three times that number. Possibly the Government may not feel inclined to print a large quantity, but I would like to know if some arrangement could not be made by which a member could get more copies of unrevised ' Hansard ' than the four which are allotted to him every day.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
I am not sure, but 1
believe that this matter is subject to regulations made by the Debates Committee. If this committee should think it desirable to make a change in the rule, I should c^tainly be pleased to adhere to their decision.

I appreciate the fact
that there must be a regulation of some kind; otherwise we would not get simply the four copies. I can understand that the officials at the Printing Bureau may require to know the number of ' Hansards ' that have to be printed. But most of us know enough about printing to know that the chief cost consists in setting up the type; when that is done the extra cost of running off three or four hundred additional copies is a mere bagatelle. If the Printing Bureau is given notice before 12 o'clock of the day after the unrevised * Hansard ' is printed, I do not see any reason why a member should not be able to obtain fifty or one hundred additional copies if he wished to have them. I do think they ought to be furnished, and when we consider the millions of dollars
that are scattered broadcast all over the city of Ottawa this is a very small matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: Of course it would only be .a small matter. If the rule is changed I know the Printing Bureau will be glad to abide by it.

Would the mimster mind making a note of it so that he can discuss it with the Chairman of the Debates Committee. I have a grievance too, and my grievance is not spasmodic, it is chronic. It costs me about $50 a session to send copies of ' Hansard ' to people who take a live interest in what is going on in the House. Sometimes, I suppose, they are disappointed but nevertheless they like to get them. I pay $3 for the 'Hansard' for a good many people, not only in my own riding, but all over the province and in other provinces as well. They say ' We are interested in what is going on in the House and would like a copy of ' Hansard.' I paid my account the other day and discovered that I am quite a philanthropist. I am not sure that the country should not pay for the dissemination of this literature, which certainly the people are entitled to. It would not require a great deal of money. My idea is that a member should be allowed at least a dozen copies a day, and I think if each member knew he could get that number he would make arrangements to have them sent to those who taken an interest in our proceedings. I send out a good many more than that, and yet do not meet all the demands because I cannot afford it.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext: I will see the Chairman of the Debates Committee about the matter.

I wish to draw the attention of the Minister to the fact that during this session and last session there has been a distribution of blue books to the members which, in my case at any rate, is not acceptable. Every morning a gentleman in the public service drives a wheelbarrow or cart up to the door of the room which four of us occupy, and insists on bringing in a large portion of the load he carries on this wheelbarrow. He deposits it in the room and goes on his way more or less rejoicing. I have tried to persuade him to keep the books but he says he has orders to deliver them at that room. I have tried every means in my power to keep these documents from being dumped into the room, but have not yet been successful. The only thing we can do is to wait until a cartload accumulates and then we issue an order to the chief whip of the basement and he proceeds to

have them taken away. What he does with them I do not know.

He sends them to our
electors.
Mr. OLIVER. That is no doulbt the intention, but I do not think our electors would read them any more than we would.
That is not my experience. My electors read them and then question me.

Some of these documents, no doubt, are interesting to the electors of my constituency, and some others to the electors of other constituencies, but I would like to have the privilege of choosing the documents to be sent to my electors. So long as the distribution office is available we can get all the documents we want for our electors, and we do not need to have the rooms we are occupying loaded up with wagon loads of material that we do not want to use. If it is necessary to get rid of that amount of printing and paper-I do not know what purpose there is in it-I would respectfully suggest that instead of insisting upon furnishing blue books that we do not read and which our constituents do not read, the number of reports of the debates could be increased to a proportionate amount. I do not say bring them in on a cart and put them in our rooms whether we want them or not, but let each man be entitled to a certain number from the distribution office. The Government would 'be no worse off, the paper mills would be called on for the same requirements, the Printing Bureau would have the same amount of work to do, and I am satisfied that the country would be better served, because, after all, there are people in Canada who have the more or less antiquated notion that the business of the country is transacted to a greater or less degree in Parliament; who are interested in the transaction of that business, and will be glad to be informed in regard to it by means of 1 Hansard.' They are quite ready to follow the proceedings of Parliament from day to day when matters of interest to them are up for consideration, but they are not prepared to go through the pages of a blue book in regard to, say, the Inland Revenue or some other department in which they do not happen to be interested. No doubt the Inland Revenue blue book is filled with facts and figures that are valuable and correct, but I do not find them interesting or informing in regard to matters in which 
I am concerned. So if the minister will arrange to have the blue books available for members at the distribution office and let them stay there until they are wanted, and will arrange for a larger number of ' Hansards,' up to a certain limit to be agreed upon, to be taken as required, he will be doing Parliament a very considerable service, and the public will not be at any greater expense, and the officers of the Administration will be at no greater inconvenience.

It seems to me that the hon. member for Edmonton is unduly critical. I am surprised that the hon. gentleman is not able to find some persons in his riding who will read these reports. I have adopted a plan in regard to these blue books and carried it out for a great many years. For instance, I get two reports of the Fisheries Department, of course, I have more than two fishermen in my county and I see that all of them, so far as I can, get a copy of that report. If it is a report of the Marine Department I send that to the marine men. I have several customs offices in my county and in order to keep them posted I send them a copy of the trade and navigation returns. I send the Postmaster General's Report to each of the postmasters in the county, and so on all along the line. I have no difficulty in getting rid of these duplicate reports-they are all issued in duplicate and, I think, without any waste. When it comes to an agricultural report you can get rid of a great many with great satisfaction. If a member does this systematically, from day to day as the reports are handed in at his door, he can dispose of these reports to advantage and without any waste. I confess that sometimes I have allowed them to accumulate for a few days or even a week but then I make a job of it, sort them all out and send them off.
But I would not like to see the number of these reports that are allotted to members curtailed. They are all required and they can be made good use of for the instruction of the public and the country generally. A member must not expect that he is going to get the fullest advantage of these reports unless he is prepared to' take a little trouble. I never employ a page to look after my ' Hansard,' I do it myself and I know it is done. I do not mean to say that the pages do not do it as well as I do. I am a believer in the old system ' if you want a tiling done, do it yourself; if you do not want it done hire somebody

else to do it.' I have for a great many years made up my own volumes of ' Hansard.' I have selected four different men in the county, who, I know, will take an interest in reading * Hansard. I use the string to bind the volume, start the volume for them and send the ' Hansard ' to them. Sometimes I am asked to send the ' Hansard ' to people. I keep every day sending the additional numbers of ' Hansard ' so that at the end of the session a man will have his volume of ' Hansard ' complete. I have done this year after year and I have found it very satisfactory. I am sure that sometimes I send the ' Hansard ' to a man who does not make as good use of it as he might, but I was told by an old farmer in my county that he read every one of them and that he was glad to get them.
Is Georgetown in that county?

Yes, it is, and I
generally see that there is one going to Georgetown.
Does it go to the quarry?
I could send it there and it would be appreciated because the people there are intelligent.

Are the quarries
working now?

My hon. friend from Pietou (Mr. Macdonald) wants to know if the quarries are running. I have not been up there for some time but I presume they are something like the coal mines in Nova Scotia; they lay off for a little while.
In both eases they bought the stuff on the other side of the line.

I am sure that one copy of the ' Hansard ' went to the quarry all
Tight.

It i.s quite possible. I see that the ' Hansards ' are scattered through the country. I take one man in one township and another man in another township and send ' Hansards ' to these men so that they will be available in different parts of the county. This is not a matter to be joked over. It is something that we ought to sympathize and do in a proper way so that through every county there will be general information given in regard to the proceedings of Parliament. If there is a political club I find the means of sending a copy of ' Hansard ' regularly to .it. To mechanics' institutes and
libraries I also send copies of the ' Hansard.1 When the session is over I have no hesitation in handing over the duplicate volumes to a library wheie the people in the to win or village have access to them. In that way the people are kept informed.
I think that the hon. member for Edmonton is very anxious to get rid of the little trouble involved in the service which he might do his constituents and which would be highly appreciated, by them. I have never received any complaints from my constituents about their having been overloaded with that sort of thing. Tney always seem to be looking for it and they want me to do it. It is surprising the amount; of information we get from these blue books.
I picked up a report, which I undertake to say not half a dozen here in this House have ever looked at-the report of the Geographic Board. I question if my hon. friend from Edmonton has ever opened that volume.
Never saw it.

Although the hon. gentleman received two volumes. I do not mean to say that I have read that volume through, but I have examined it, and I have picked out something in it that I thought was erroneous. I have written letters to the secretary of the Geographic Board calling attention to the errors that they made in the changing of names, and I got their reply. If I had not been satisfied with the reply I would have made another appeal. In one instance, not long ago, I had a promise that the matter would again be brought before the board. We can make use of these documents if we only devote a little time to the matter. I would not advise the Secretary of State, or whoever has control of the publication of these volumes, to curtail the number. I am always pleased to see the cart unloaded at my door and the quota that is allowed to me, thrown off, ready for distribution. I may be a little late sometimes in sending them away, but I always see that they are got away before the session closes. I think it is a very good plan, to keep your people informed, and if you do they will appreciate it.

We appreciate the very kind advice which the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) has given us, but he must remember that we are not all as industrious as he is. It is pretty hard for ordinary mortals to carry out the programme which my hon. friend prescribes

for us. There is no doubt that if we would work as hard as he does we would be able to disseminate a large amount of information among our constituents which would be of very great value to them. I think that perhaps he did not understand or appreciate the point made by my hon. friend from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver). My hon. friend wanted the documents printed, but he wanted the right to go and say what he wanted to have. If my hon. friend from Edmonton did not want the Geographic Board reports, my hon. friend from Halton would be welcome to them. But I want to come back to the innocent question which I asked of the minister and which started this discussion. I appreciate that it would not be fair to ask the department to publish, say, fifty copies of ' Hansard ' for every member every day. I doubt very much if that quantity would be taken care of by the members and sent out to their destinations. I would, however, suggest that some arrangement be made by which, if a member gave notice by noon of the next day, he could get fifty or one hundred copies. I was never in the Printing Bureau, but I presume the type must be kept there until the revised ' Hansard ' is issued. If it be there until, say, next day at noon, there should be no trouble in striking off whatever number of copies a member wants. In that way you might supply different members with what they required at a nominal cost to the country. I think that four to each member is not sufficient. I generally send out the ' Hansard/ and I have done so since I have been in Parliament. The persistency of my hon. friend from Halton and myself may be some reason why some other hon. gentlemen are sometimes short of ' Hansards.'
No, I never stole anything belonging to another man.

However, let that be as it may, it is only another argument in favour of having more printed. I hope that my hon. friend the Secretary of State will appreciate the request I am making and see if something cannot be done to comply with it.

I quite agree with my hon. friend from South Renfrew (Mr. Graham) and my hon. friend from Carleton (Mr. Carvell), that more discretion should be given to the distribution office in supplying members of the House who require a larger number of ' Hansards.' I do not say that the daily edition of ' Hansard ' i-Mr. Carvell.]
should be increased in number, but a certain discretion should be used in regard to the distribution of a larger number when needed. Since we are speaking about ' Hansard,' I must congratulate the ' Hansard ' staff on the improvement that has been made this year in the Official Report of the Debates of the House. On the first page of ' Hansard ' you will find the word ' Canada,' which formerly did not appear there, and you will also find enumerated the subject matters of the day's debate, which is a new feature. Then, there is printed the name of ouf venerable Speaker, who was ignored in former years so far as ' Hansard ' is concerned.
That is the only way he has to get his name on 'Hansard.'

Then the hours appear, and you will find printed at the side of the column '4 p.m.' or '5 p.m./ as the case may be, which facilitates search. May I ask the Secretary of State if the Chief of the French translators has been appointed? I belong to the Debates Committee, but I find that our functions have been singularly curtailed of late. It seems to me that we should not be treated in that way. We are interested in having an excellent report of the speeches in the House, and generally speaking ' Hansard ' is well produced and is a credit to Canada, but I regret to say that the French version is not up to date. We have on the staff some excellent translators like Mr. Lasalle, Mr. Gorin, Mr, Hughes, Mr. LaRose, Mr. Gascon, and others whose names I forget, but unfortunately one or two have been appointed of late who are not up to the mark. I showed the Postmaster General one translation of one of my speeches, and it nearly turned his hair grey. This translation was made by a gentleman who has been recently appointed. Whether he passed the examination or not I do not know, but the important point is that the chief translator has resigned, and is now an ordinary member of the staff. As a translator he is excellent, but he had no authority over his staff. Some time ago the translators' staff unanimously signed a petition asking that Mr. Lucien Lasalle should be appointed chief. Mr. Lasalle is no political friend of mine. He is a well-known friend of the present Administration; but it is a question of ability and not politics. It is well known that Mr. Lasalle possesses ability and amiability as well; he is the oldest translator there; he was appointed in the

earlier eighties; he has authority over the staff, and I am sure that if he were appointed he would see where the laches are at present, and that no manuscript should go out of the office until it were sufficiently revised even for the unrevised edition.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: This has nothing to do with the Secretary of State.

We were speaking of
public documents, and, anyway I have almost concluded. I would like the Postmaster General, the Secretary of State, and the Minister of Inland Revenue to take this matter into serious consideration and to confer with Mr. Speaker. I do not introduce any politics into this. I belong to the Debates Committee and have at heart the preservation of a good. French report of our debates. I trust that Mr. Lasalle will be appointed, and if not, Mr. Gerin-Lajoie, or Mr. Hughes, or Mr. Gascon, who are all able. But, the senior is Mr. Lasalle and he should be given promotion. As it is at present I make bold to say that there are many pages of ' Hansard ' which are really a discredit to the French language.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext:
This matter does not come under the control of the Secretary of State. I think we should heartily congratulate Mr. Speaker for the care he has taken and the success he has achieved in endeavouring to secure a first-class staff for the translation of ' Hansard '. It is only due to Mr. Speaker that I should say so. I do not controvert for one moment that some parts of the speech of my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux) were poorly translated, but the translation was not quite bad enough to turn my hair grey, as he said. I would not like it to be thought that Mr. Speaker has not achieved success in his efforts to secure a competent staff, and as a matter of fact, and without giving any name, one of the first-class men on the staff was ill at the time, and he was replaced by a gentleman who translated the speech of my hon. friend about which complaint has been made. This gentleman is not a permanent member of the staff, and I understand that he is not going to be retained. I wish my hon. friend to know this so that there may be no discredit cast on the permanent staff.
As I said, I am not going to give any particular names, but this gentleman is not qualified. As a member of the Board of Internal Economy, I desire to express to my hon. friend my sincere regret that the speech which he made on that occasion, and which was an important speech, was not translated as it should have been-My hon. friend from Rouville will admit with me that the work of that staff is very well done as a rule.
Has the chief of that staff been appointed permanently or temporarily?

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Mr. Trudel is temporarily in charge.

I have nothing to say
against Mr. Trudel; he is a good translator.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: The Speaker of the House is taking a keen interest in this matter. He is trying to do the best he can in regard to it and for the moment Mr. Trudel, who is a great acquisition and a credit to the staff, is acting temporarily. The suggestions made by my hon. friend within the hearing of the Speaker of this House will be for the Speaker to consider. I understand that the Speaker last year was asked to give Mr. Lasalle some help on account of illness. Mr. Gerin is also a very good man; but on the whole I think that we may safely expect that the efforts made so far will be continued, and that the members will have occasion to congratulate themselves on very great improvement in that staff.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member foi
Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) has found fault with the distribution of blue books in the rooms of the members. The Printing Bureau has nothing to do with that. All that the Printing Bureau has to do is to deliver the books here, to the Clerk of the House. I am told by the Clerk that it is not his fault either. Last year there was a very large room for the distribution of the blue books. That room has been given to the members, and the Clerk has now no room in which to place those blue books when they come in, and has to take other means to distribute them.

Put them in the clerk's room.
Miscellaneous printing, $100,000.
Mr. Oliver:	In regard to additional
copies of ' Hansard,' would it be possible to issue an order that would 11 p.m. enable members to get up, say, a dozen copies of the unrevised ' Hansard,' should we ask for them, or to make a further arrangement that by giving a notice we could get up to say 50 or 100 copies as the case might be? Suppos-

ing some special question came up of interest to my constituents, it would be in the public interest that I should be in a position to inform my constituents in regard to the matter. If it was arranged that an order would be honoured up to 50 or 100 or whatever number of copies might be decided upon, it would be distinctly in the interest of the people.

The Secretary of State has nothing to do with that. I will see the chairman of the Debates Committee an regard to the matter, and I am sure that, if he will frame a rule that will be approved by the House, the Printing Bureau will act in accordance with it.
Progress reported.
On motion of Mr. Rogers the House adjourned at 11.10 p.m.
Wednesday, March 18, 1914.
